The morning newspapers announce that there has been another case at Cornwall of shooting by a sentry of some innocent people. Has any news reached the department about it?

I suppose that it is on the strength of the newspaper despatch that the right hon. gentleman speaks of these people as innnocent. It is always well to wait before reaching a conclusion. I have seen the item, just as the right hon. gentleman has seen it, but I have no further information on the subject. The people in the locality have been instructed when challenged to halt; also to obey the orders of the soldiers; otherwise, the soldiers cannot carry on their work. It must be remembered that the sentry has no easy job.

And it is
stated that the sentries are instructed to shoot to kill.

On motion of Hon. Frank Cochrane (Minister of Railways and Canals), the House went into committee on Bill No. 119, to amend the National Transcontinental Railway Act, Mr. Sevigny in the Chair.
On the preamble:

This matter was pretty
thoroughly discussed on the resolution, hut, for the sake of clearness, I wish to state my position again. In the first place, some-arrangement should be made for the operation of the Transcontinental until such time as it is completed. The duty of the Government, in my humble judgment, is not to pass this measure to expropriate the property of the Grand Trunk Pacific or of any other company that it desires to expropriate; but immediately, with all possible speed, to complete the eastern division of the Transcontinental, which is not at present completed according to the agreement with the company.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
When is it
completed according to the agreement?

When the agreement is fulfilled; it certainly is not completed when the terminals at Quebec are not constructed-leaving other matters out of consideration for the time. The award of Sir William Whyte was that all the shops are necessary for the operation of the road.
I was pointing out the duty of the Government to complete the National Transcontinental, so far as the Quebec terminals at least are concerned, and so to be in a position to tell the company: we have fulfilled our part of the agreement, now take over the line or certain proceedings will be taken. Until such time as the project is completed, the step proposed under this legislation is premature.
I do not know that I can add much more. I discussed the matter at some length when the House was in committee on the resolution. It does seem to me that the Government is altogether in advance of the situation which has been created by itself in not completing the work. In the city of Quebec, a line has been purchased from the Canadian Northern Railway for the standardizing of which a grant is now asked in the Estimates. The station in Quebec is not begun; the shops are just started; the small station at Champlain market is only nicely begun. As a matter of fact, there is nothing in Quebec to take care of the Quebec traffic under this agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. It has been stated that the fact that the Quebec bridge is not completed may be suggested bv the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company as a reason for their not taking over the road.

That contention will not stand for a moment before any tribunal when the documents are produced.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: To what documents does the hon. gentleman refer?

I refer to a letter sent
to the Railway Department by Mr. Hays himself, in which he admitted that the company would consider the operation of a ferry at Quebec as fulfilment of the contract providing for a continuous line. That letter was received by the Railway Department and was left by me in that department.
It is not there now.
That is not my fault; it ought to be there.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What is the date of that letter?
I cannot say at this time. I remember distinctly receiving the letter, taking it to Council, showing it to the Prime Minister and having it filed in the department.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: About what date?

It was some time before Mr. Hays' death. It was written by Mr. Hays in connection with some other correspondence, and I think a careful search will result in its being found in the department. I am prepared to say that such a letter was received. As I have pointed out, I think the Government should complete the project so that the company will have no reasonable grounds for objection on that score, and then, if the company do not proceed to fulfil their contract, that will be the proper time to take such steps as may be deemed necessary. At the present time, however, I think it is inopportune for the Government to pass legislation giving them powers which, to my mind, they are not in a position to act upon without violating the agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, because the Government, in my humble judgment, has not completed the project according to the agreement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The Government already has a substantial portion of the powers set forth in this amendment, inasmuch as last year it was provided by an Act then passed that, until the Grand Trunk Pacific railway should accept a lease and undertake operation, the Minister of Railways and Canals might himself operate the
road. The present legislation carries that further, in this respect; that it gives to the Minister of Railways, subject to the approval of the Governor in Council, authority to lease a branch line which would be an essential portion of the eastern division of the National Transcontinental railway. It supplies that which was left unprovided for in the Act of last year, and it tnoroughly subserves the purpose which was intended to be accomplished by that Act. That Act, if I remember correctly, received the unanimous assent of the House.
That is all right, but this proposed legislation goes farther than that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In what way?

It takes power otherwise to acquire-that means, to expropriate- that line from the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company; to expropriate its terminals or terminals belonging to any other company. One of the points I endeavoured to raise was that if the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company then proposed to take over the line, the Government would find itself the owner of all these terminals, and the line as well.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As a matter of fact, it was contended-and I thought it was a well-founded contention-that so important a branch as the Lake Superior branch might very well belong to the Government, assuming that the Government were to have ownership, as it has ownership, of the whole of the eastern division from Moncton to Winnipeg. The objection that my hon. friend makes is based, I understand, on the suggestion that the Government may expropriate. I am not at all sure that the word " acquire " would have that meaning.
That is the construction that was put upon it by the Solicitor General.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is possible that it might bear that construction, but I should rather think that if power ito expropriate were to be conferred, some words of a more definite character would be used. I was not here during the discussion, and was not aware that my hon. friend the Solicitor General had expressed that opinion. The authority to take away, against his will, the common law property or rights of any citizen in this or any other country, even at the instance of the Crown, must be couched in' very express terms. Further

than that, it is a very familiar principle that even if compensation is not provided for in the act of expropriation, the courts *will always construe any such statute as contemplating compensation to the extent of the value of the property and ten per cent additional. My toon, friend says that this legislation is inopportune. There is something that would ibe very much more inopportune and unfortunate, namely, that this road being in effect complete for all practical purposes, although it may not toe technically completed within the meaning of the Act, should remain unoperated. That is the reason why the Government introduced last year, and has introduced again this year, legislation to prevent that particular condition being brought about. Any horn, gentleman would find it exceedingly difficult to look at the legislation and the contracts of 1903-4 and come to a conclusion as to what the completion of that road meant, within the meaning of that legislation and those contracts. As a matter of fact, a railway, in one sense, is never complete. There has not been a year since the Canadian Pacific railway has been completed that work of an important character has not been done upon it; particularly is this true of the last twenty years. The Grand Trunk Pacific railway has 'been operated in the West for three or four years; it has been handling large passenger and freight traffic, although as yet it is not technically completed-a long way from it. Would my hon. friend suggest that under those circumstances a railway, although not absolutely technically completed, ought to remain unoperated? Does he suggest that it is in the interests of the people of the country that it should remain unoperated? We have taken the responsibility of deciding that any such condition would be most unfortunate, and detrimental to the public interest. We are not looking forward to any controversy with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company in regard to this matter, but it is necessary to make provision for that which might possibly occur. Suppose it were suggested to the company: this road is as complete as the road which has been operated in the West *for three or four years; while it may not be technically complete, nevertheless it is for all practical purposes complete within the meaning of this Act, and it is your duty to proceed to take a lease and to operate. If the company raised the contention that they are not bound to operate that road until such and such absolute conditions have been complied with, we find that the contract" and the

statutes of 1903-4, unfortunately, contain no provisions definitely determining the matter. I am not iquite sure that if such a question arose it might be determined toy arbitration; otherwise iit would have to toe determined toy the courts. In either case there would be very considerable delay. In the case of a determination by the courts, two or three yeaTS might be involved. We want to avoid all that. We have no desire or intention of having any controversy ot difficulty with the company, and we do not propose to look forward to anything of the kind. My own attitude-and this has been the attitude of the Government as well since we came into power-has been to deal with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company in respect of this enterprise precisely in the same way and to extend to them precisely the same consideration in every respect as if the enterprise had been initiated by the party which is now charged with the responsibilities of office, and I venture to state that no instance can toe found in which that policy has been departed from.
With respect to what my hon. friend *suggests about the Quebec bridge, I do not desire to apprehend that any unfair or unreasonable difficulty will he caused by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. I am not going to apprehend anything of the kind until it actually occurs. But we must not be blind to the consideration that a contract formally executed under the authority of the board of directors and sanctioned by a vote of the shareholders cannot legally be set aside or modified by a letter from Mr. Hays as president of that road; at least that is my present impression. The contract of 1903-4 was executed under the .authority of the board of directors of the company. The board of directors of the company, if I remember correctly, were required to place the contract before the shareholders. That contract, made in that way, with these legal formalities, might not be changed, .so far .as its legal effect is concerned, by the mere letter of the president of the road, however important his position or however extensive his authority. We have to take into account considerations of that kind. We discussed the matter in a very friendly way with the officials of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway company, and, unless I am mistaken, the legislation was submitted to them either in the exact form in which it is now presented to the House or in .a form substantially the same; and, as far as my

knowledge of the attitude of the company goes, they have not any desire to oppose it, nor, as far as I understand, do they oppose it in any way. It is a reasonable precaution which we are taking for the purpose of preventing the road from remaining without operation during a period in which some question might reasonably be raised by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway company as to its duty to take over the road for operation and as to the right of the Government to enforce that operation.

The only correspondence which has been submitted to the House is simply to show that there is a disagreement between the company and the Government, now representing the commission of construction, as to whether or not the road is completed according to the terms of the contract. That is all the information that we have before us. My right hon. friend stated a moment ago that the company does not offer any objection to this legislation. That may be. In his absence the other day the Minister of Railways stated that the company were anxious to hand over this road to the Government-that they did not desire to operate it. That also may ibe true. But of this we have no information, and my hon. friend knows that is not the way to deal with Parliament-to give word of mouth. We should have correspondence and written documents and evidence upon that point. I do not question the word of the Minister of Railways at all; I am not prepared to say that Mx. Chambenldn, the president of the company, did not say what was attributed to him; tout I would like to know the circumstances under which Mr. Chamberlin made that suggestion. As to this we have no evidence. The only thing we have before us is that there is a disagreement between the engineers of the company and the engineers of the Government as to the completion of the road.
I shall not go over the discussion we had the other day; but in our judgment, which I think is fully sustained by the statute in that behalf, whenever a question of this kind arises the method of settlement provided by the statute is arbitration. My hon. friend stated a moment ago that the road, while completed in a sense, may never be completed. I know the Canadian Pacific railway may be truly said not to be completed,' because it is a matter of notoriety that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has been building and rebuilding its line again and again. But
my hon. friend knows that the intention of the engineers charged with the work was to build this railway once for all. And now my hon. friend asks, how are we going to determine that? There is an easy way of determining it. The plans and specifications were prepared by the company and the Government together, they were joint specifications, and everything was done under the signatures of both engineers. The question now is whether or not the work contemplated by those specifications is completed. If the work is .completed, then the company can be compelled to take over the road. If there is a disagreement between the engineers, I repeat, we can go to arbitration. I can understand that the company is not anxious to take over the road. I gave reasons the other day. The company has been treated most contemptuously in this matter. My hon. friend says the company has been treated with every consideration possible. That may be. I know, of course, that the Government has advanced aid to the company by way of loans on more than one occasion; but as to the construction of the road, and the terminals at Quebec especially, while I do not know what issue they take with the Government, the company cannot but feel that they have been treated with great contempt and in defiance of their legitimate rights and aspirations. My hon. friend knows the details, but I do not suppose that it is disputed that shops and terminals are essential to a railway, and the company cannot be asked to take over the railway and operate it unless it has been provided with terminals. Terminals are just as essential for the operating of the road as the road bed itself. The Quebec terminals, which were provided for by the company and the commission of that day on a joint agreement satisfactory to both, have been simply discarded by the present Administration and another agreement substituted.
The Minister of Railways stated the other day that they have provided foT joint terminals at Quebec, with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I take issue with him and say that -such a union station, placed in the valley of the St. Charles river and not in the valley of the St. Lawrence, cannot be as useful to the company as the station which we had provided for. Let that stand for the time being. I refreshed my memory by reading the contract with the Canadian Pacific railway, as brought down by the Government itself, and what do I fin'd? I find that the agreement

between the Government and the Canadian Pacific railway for the union station contemplates and provides only for a terminal for the Grand Trunk Pacific railroad, and that the Grand Trunk Railway Company itself, the parent company of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, is excluded from that agreement. Can anybody imagine that the Grand Trunk Pacific will accept as satisfactory an agreement for joint terminals for the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific, and not for the Grand Trunk railway itself? It cannot agree to that. Up to the present time, so far as I know, it has refused to accept that agreement, because not a tittle of evidence has been produced to show that the company ever acceded to the demand made by the Minister of Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for these joint terminals. It is not surprising, therefore, that under the circumstances the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company -should say: the contract has not been lived up to, and we are not in a position to take over the road. I would think that the best way to settle the matter would be by arbitration; but that may take some time. Whether the position of the company is well founded or not, there is a disagreement between the company and the Government. So far so good -or so bad. My hon. friend says that the road must be operated. Certainly; we agree that the road must be operated. Last year when the Government asked for legislation to operate the road, pending the settlement of these difficulties, we offered not a word of objection, but agreed that the road must be operated; and to-day we say that the road must be operated.
But I should like to call the attention of my hon. friend to the fact that this legislation which he is submitting is not of a temporary but of a permanent character. Let me read the legislation which we axe now asked to sanction, and then ask whether it has not altogether the appearance of permanent legislation so designed that ihe Government can take possession of the road and operate it itself. If such be the intent of the Government, we should like to know it. I did not draw that conclusion from the remarks made by my right hon. friend a moment ago. No other interpretation can be placed upon this legislation than that it is intended to enable the Government to take over the ownership of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Let me read the section:

The Minister of Railways and Canals may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, lease or otherwise acquire-
We discussed these words " or otherwise acquire " with the Solicitor General the other day, and in his opinion they were broad enough to cover the case of expropriation, if that were necessary. Of course, an agreement may be entered into which would render expropriation proceedings unnecessary.
The Minister of Railways and Canals may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, lease or otherwise acquire that portion of the railway of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company known as the Lake Superior branch, extending from Lake Superior Junction to the city of Port William in Ontario, including terminal facilities and accommodation works of the said company or of any other company, and for all the purposes of this section may provide, by purchase, lease or otherwise, rolling stock and equipment; and the- Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and such other company is each hereby authorized on its part to deal accordingly with the said line of railway or terminal facilities and accommodation works as the case may be.
I say that no interpretation can be placed on these words other than that the Government intends to acquire the Grand Trunk Pacific, either by expropriation, purchase or otherwise, and to operate the enterprise itself.

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK COCHRANE (Minister of Railways and Canals) :
speechtext: In the debate the other day I think we discussed pretty fully the question of the non-completion of the road. I must take exception to the statement of the ex-Mdnister of Railways (Mr. Graham), that there is ample provision in Quebec for all the traffic. As I stated the other day, we have entered -into an arrangement with the Canadian Pacific Railway by which we cannot only use the Canadian Pacific railway terminals, station, yards and so on, but also run right down to the docks built by the Government.
The Government has built no docks there.

The docks were built by the Harbour Commissioners, who are practically the Government. Whoever operates the road has to get down to the docks, and if we had not made this arrangement we should have had to expropriate a tremendous amount of valuable property in order to get down to the docks. I take issue with the statement of the leader of the Opposition that the Act provides that the question of the completion of the road

shall be settled by arbitration. The only -thing it says about arbitration is that the engineers can be called in to arbitrate on the construction of any portion, of the line. Nothing at all is said about arbitrating on the completion of the road. Take the Grand Trunk Pacific at Edmonton. They have no route through Edmonton now, and no facilities, yet they are operating there, and most successfully, I think. They are running one of the best trains between Edmonton and Winnipeg that tihere is in Canada to-day.
The Grand Trunk Pacific have made arrangements at Edmonton. They have freight arrangements of their own.
They have no through arrangements in Edmonton, and have never pretended that they have.
I beg to correct the minister. They have freight arrangements of their own.
Where is their passenger station in Edmonton for their terminals? Where do they get through Edmonton?
They get through by an arrangement with the Canadian Northern railway.
We do not know anything about that arrangement. It has never been brought before Parliament or before the Department of Railways or before the Railway Commission.
Has the agre-ment with the Canadian Pacific railway at Quebec been brought before Parliament?

No. But they do
not want to get out of it, or intend to get out of it. As far as the Lake Superior branch is concerned, I claim that as a matter of policy it should never belong to the Grand Trunk Pacific. It should belong to the owners of the Transcontinental. It is the key to the West. As I stated in a previous debate we are not desirous of operating the Transcontinental. We want the company to take it over. Year by year we shall have to work on capital account to improve the road. On the portion of the road between lake Superior and Winnipeg, which was completed by the late Government, there are wooden trestles that will have to be strengthened in some way or filled. That will be a capital charge. The ex-Minister of Railways has made a point
in regard to Mr. Hay's letter in reference to the Quebec bridge. But the leader of the Government says that a letter is no good because it is not a document.
A letter is a document.

It is not a legal document. As has been stated by the leader of the Government, it would not commit the company if we were to take a legal opinion on it. The right hon. leader of the Opposition has also referred to the specifications. Now there are hundreds of classes in those specifications, as to which half a dozen different opinions could be held. The engineers themselves cannot agree as to the meaning of some parts of the specifications. If we were to say that the contract had been completed according to specifications, I think we should have a hard time to substantiate that before a court. The terminals at Fort William are not owned by the Grand Trunk Pacific; they are owned by a separate company. I am not so sure whether the elevator is owned by another company or not, but the terminals are. That is the reason they are mentioned in this way in the Bill. I am sure that my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, or the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, will admit that we would be very foolish to attempt to operate this road without having the right to the use of the branch down to Fort William. I made the statement the other day, and I know it will not be denied, that Mr. Chamberlin, now the president of the road, told me- I will take his word for it and I will get a document from him for it-that he would agree to any terms that we might arrange with the Canadian Pacific Railway and others. He said that he would accept those terms, and he will not go back on that. I should say in fairness to him though, that, while he does not approve of the arrangement, still he will not go back on the agreement. I claim the road is fully completed for operation. We have provided in Quebec for every part of the operation there. As for the suggestion that the shops have not been completed, let me tell the committee that they have not a shop on the whole 1,800 miles from Winnipeg to Prince Rupert except small shops which they have at the divisional points. I made the statement the other day, and I repeat it now, that at every divisional point from Winnipeg to Moncton we have shops far superior to any that they have on their part of the road; yet they have operated more than half of that road now for four years.

On the mountain section they have only four divisional points with very few stations or yards equipped, and
12 noon, yet they are operating to probably as great an extent as we will operate in the East unless business improves during the next year. My hon. friend takes the ground that the terminals at Quebec will not be equal to the terminals formerly proposed. I am satisfied that, both in the interest of the railway and of the business community at Quebec, the change in the terminals will prove to be a desirable one. We are building down into the city of Quebec for the purpose of taking care of the business there. We believe that the harbour of Quebec will be much more important than it has ever been in the past. In order to be able to participate in the business at Quebec, and to compete with the Canadian Pacific railway and other roads, it was necessary for us to get down to the Louise Basin.

My hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals is very inconsistent in so far as his dealing with the president of the Grand Trunk Pacific is concerned, because in connection with the Quebec bridge he says that the country is not safe in taking the letter of the president.

I only referred to that in connection with the statement of my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals and my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. They said that the president was doubtless morally bound to stand by that letter of the former president.
Not at all.

As far as the bridge is concerned, I understand that the question came up when the late Government was in office and that the president of the company, acting for the company and speaking in the name of the company, expressly waived the matter of the completion of the Quebec bridge as essential to the completion of the contract. The minister seems doubtful as to whether that would be binding. The way to ascertain whether it would be binding or not is to request the president of the company to have the board of directors, or shareholders, ratify it and put it in the form of a contract. I cannot see why that has not been done by this Government. One would think that during the nearly four years that they have been in office, in a matter of such vast importance as this, if they had any doubt as to the company being bound by th? letter of the
[Mr. Cochrane.!
president, they would have taken steps to have that matter confirmed and the letter put in proper legal form. But while the minister says there is doubt as to the binding character of that letter, when ft comes to another question, the question of the changes in the terminals, the changes in the location of the workshops at Quebec and the changes in. the grades of the road, the minister says that the president has told him so and so and that he will take his word for it, showing that when the minister wants to rely upon the word of the president he is quite willing to take his word, but when he does not want to rely on an assurance of the president he does not want to taka his letter.
The hon. gentleman is unfair to me in that respect.
In what respect?
In what the hon. gentleman has just said. I was only making a comparison.

I accept the minister's statement, but after all is it not all nonsense for the Government to keep the country and Parliament in doubt as to these verbal statements and as to these statements by letter? Why have they not put the matter in writing? The minister knows perfectly well that the road must be built according to the specifications which were agreed upon. It is of enormous importance in connection with a road that is going to cost this country, according to the hon. gentleman, something like $50,000,000-
How many?
Something like $50,000,000.
What?

Something like $50,000,-
000.
Fifty million?

Yes, making allowance for interest for seven years, and assuming, of course, that the road will be self-sustaining after that. It is of very great importance and one would hav.e thought that the Government would have taken steps to have had the waiver condition as to the Quebec bridge put in proper form.
That only came up quite recently.

That only came up
quite recently? How could it help coming up? It must have been in the mind of the minister from the time he took office. Here is the gap of the Quebec bridge not completed, and it will not be completed for a number of years, across which the traffic will be carried by ferry. It never came up, says the minister, and yet he asked this Parliament for an appropriation to establish a car ferry at Quebec. One would have thought that it would have come to the minister's mind at once. When he was asking Parliament for authority to engage in an expenditure of $1,000,000 or more, one would have thought that the question of making an agreement in writing in order to carry out the assurance of the president that the establishment of a ferry would be regarded as a completion of the line would have been uppermost in his mind.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister has stated that so far as he knows the company has no objection to this legislation. Surely there is another question involved besides what may be the wishes of the company. This committee knows very well that when it was proposed to construct the Transcontinental railway, the Grand Trunk Pacific wanted to stop at North Bay and did not want to have anything to do with a line east of North Bay. They recognized that it was the prairie section, the section between the foothills of the Rocky mountains and the head of the Great Lakes, which would be the profitable portion of the line, and they felt that if, in the summer season, they could bring their freight and a great many of their passengers to Fort William and carry them down over the lakes to their connection with the Grand Trunk railway at Sarnia, it would be much more profitable to them, and that if they could get a connection at North Bay so as to bring their all-rail traffic down to the junction with the Grand Trunk there, and in this way carry the produce of the West over the Grand Trunk to the Grand Trunk ports, it would be more advantageous to the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific. But the Government, led by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), insisted from the very commencement that the road must be carried right through to Moncton, where it would join the Intercolonial and over which the traffic could be distributed to the ports of the Maritime Provinces. That was regarded as onerous by the Grand Trunk Pacific, but the Government insisted, and rightly insisted, upon it.
One could very well understand that, if the Grand Trunk Pacific could be let out of this bargain as far as the line east of Winnipeg is concerned, if they could get many millions of dollars under expropriation for their terminals at Fort William and still be allowed to use the line as far east as Fort William and to abandon all idea of operating the main line between Winnipeg and Moncton, that proposition might commend itself to the Grand Trunk Pacific and enable them to carry out the ideas which they entertained at the commencement, but which the late Government prevented them from carrying into effect. Therefore, apart from the Grand Trunk Pacific, there is involved the important question of having a" transcontinental line operated by one company carrying the traffic between the East and the West, between the Atlantic and the Pacific, that company operating all parts of that line and developing, as a great transcontinental railway company can develop, the country through which it passes. Speaking for the Maritime Provinces, I desire to enter my most earnest protest against any proposition that will lead the Grand Trunk Pacific to believe that it may be released from the operation of the eastern section of the Transcontinental. That is what this proposition is looking to, that is, for the Government to' expropriate the line between Lake Superior Junction and Fort William, to become the owner of it, and then with what justice, with what reason-
Should we not be the owner of it when we own the other line?
Not at all.
I am glad the country knows that.

There is not the slightest reason why we should be the owner of it. The Government does not own a single branch of the Transcontinental railway anywhere; it owns no branch betweeen Ottawa and the Transcontinental, between Montreal and the Transcontinental, nor between St. John and the Transcontinental. The idea which the late Government had in view was to construct one main line that was to be leased to the Grand Trunk Pacific for a period of fifty years. That company were to become the operators of the line, and an Act passed at the time

gave them power to construct branch lines and also provided what should be done with the branch lines in case at the end of the fifty years the Government should take over the operation of the main line. That was all clearly provided for; but let the Government under the power granted by this legislation take over the line between Superior Junction and Fort William, and, I ask, with what justice or reason could the Grand Trunk Pacific be compelled to enter upon the operation of the main line?
My hon. friend says that there is no power conveyed in the Act to determine when the line is completed. I must confess that I have heard many extraordinary statements made in this House, although not by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways, who says so few things that he is not apt to say anything extraordinary. He is careful and uses good judgment; but- he is led astray to-day, and he makes a most extraordinary statement when he says that the provision in section 7 of the Act of 1903, which says that any question as to the work-
As to the work?

Yes-that any question as to the work in regard to which the engineers differ shall be left to arbitration, applies to all matters during construction, but has no application to the question of the completion of the line. In other words, up to fifteen minutes before the last bit of ballast is put in, the engineers have everything to do with the question whether the line is built right up to the specifications or not; but at the last minute, when the last shovelful or the last carload of ballast is put in, the jurisdiction of the engineers and the third arbitrator, whom they are to appoint, absolutely ceases, and they have no power to say whether the road has been built according to the specifications or not. I would not have thought it possible, but for the respect that I have for the good judgment of my hon. friend the minister, for me to believe that any gentleman of good judgment would make a statement like that in this House. As I said the other day, take the case of a man building a house, which is a matter of large importance, the owner has his architect, and the contractor has his architect to look after the work. It is provided that the house must be built according to the specifications agreed upon; that the work must be done under the joint supervision of the two architects and upon their joint
fMr. Pugsley. ]
inspection and joint acceptance, and that if there shall arise between the two architects any question as to the work upon which they cannot agree, they shall choose a third arbitrator, and if they fail to choose one, he shall be Chosen by the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court. Surely, if the question arose between the two architects whether the house were entirely completed according to the specification's or not, that would be a case for calling in a third arbitrator to determine that question.

Is there not a very well-decided case on record in Hudson on building contracts, that the power given to arbitrators to determine whether ot not work done is done in accordance with the specifications does not cover the power to determine whether or not it is completed? There is a very clear distinction between the work and the completion.
I do not think so, and I doubt very much if my hon. friend can produce authority to that effect.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There are some legal men in this country who probably would be almost if not quite as capable of forming an opinion upon this as even my hon. friend, and who do not entertain the same view as he does.	.

During my professional career, I have always had great respect for the opinion of others, and I have often found that their opinions have prevailed; but still all that I can do is to state my own view-that is what I have always endeavoured to do in discussing legal propositions-and then leave it to the court to determine whether my view is correct or not. I would be surprised to find that any court o,r any lawyer of high standing would determine that, where a question of having the work done according to the specifications arises, and all authority is given to the engineers as to supervision, inspection and acceptance and the provision as to what shall be done in case of a difference shall have to do with everything in connection with the work up to the completion of it, and yet have nothing to do with the completion. That which has led the Minister of Railways astray, I think, is that he thinks of a railway as different from an ordinary work. For instance, a house, he would say, is completed when it is built according to the specifications, and nothing further need be done; but a railway is con-

stantly expanding and new work will be required, and therefore, according to his view, a railway can never be said to be " completed " in the sense in which a house is " completed." But you must read the word in connection with the specifications. When the work is done according to the specifications, that work is " completed " under tlhe terms of the contract. Suppose that the specifications did not provide for water-tanks. If the Government builds the road according to the specifications and without water-tanks, that road is " completed-" under the contract, and if the company wants water-tanks they must put them in themselves. The word " completed " in section 20 of the Act means completed in accordance with the specifications.
Now, the Act provides that when the road is completed the company shall be called upon to enter into the lease. That means, it seems to me, as clearly as words can make it, when the contract is completed according to specifications.
Where is the clause authorizing the building of tihe shops at all?
I understand that the specifications provide for the building of the shops.
No.

Then, if that is the case, I think the hon. gentleman should slhow that everything required by the. specifications has been done-that the grades, the curves, the workshops, the terminals, are made according to the specifications-and his engineer would be able to say that the road is " completed."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If the specifications left out a bridge, would the same result follow?

That is putting a very
extreme case.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: You have to test the argument by these extreme cases.

It would not be a railway if the bridge were left out. In a case like that, I think the course would be to dismiss both engineers and try to get out of the difficulty as best you could. But the point I have sought to make, and it may be that I am entirely wrong through being very stupid-is that it seems absolutely clear to me that under the statute "completion" of the line, means
completion according to the specifications. Let me use again the illustration I gave the other day: Suppose the Minister of Railways had given the company a subsidy to be paid on the completion of its line of railway, specifications being provided. Surely, if the road is not perfect, yet, when the specifications are complied with the minister could not refuse to pay that subsidy. He pays the subsidy when his engineer reports that the specifications have been complied with. That is what is meant by the "completion" of the railway.
Let me add just a word before I resume my seat, to emphasize in the strongest way possible, the mistake that this Government, in my opinion, is making, in not asking the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to enter upon the temporary operation of this line pending the completion of the entire road in accordance with the specifications. I charge the Minister of Railways with not treating this House fairly, with not treating the country fairly. Two years ago I brought this matter up and called his attention, and the attention of the Prime Minister, to the fact that the late president of the road, Mr. Hays, had made an offer to the Government to take over the road as the different portions were completed and to operate the line, providing the necessary rolling stock, upon a basis of which no one could complain. Let me repeat it again, in view of this extraordinary legislation, so that no one can forget it. The offer was that they would put on their own rolling stock; they would operate the line under Government supervision; the whole business should be subject to the audit of the Government, and if there was any profit from the operation that profit should be handed over to the treasury of the country, and if there was a deficit, the amount should be added to the capital account on which the company would pay interest as it was to pay interest on the whole cost of the line. I called the attention of the minister to this offer, and he stated in this House that he would take the matter up with the Grand Trunk Pacific and see if they were still willing to enter into an agreement of that kind, and inform the House at a later date. Up to this moment he has not made any statement to this House that the Grand Trunk Pacific had been approached with a view to entering upon the operation of the -completed portions of the line lupon these terms. And, though this committee has no information

that there has been any effort to get the Grand Trunk Pacific to enter upon the temporary operation of the line, pending its entire completion, when they will be obliged to enter into the formal lease, the minister comes here to-day and asks authority to involve this country in an expenditure of many millions for rolling stock to enable the Government to operate the line, and to incur an expenditure of many millions further to acquire the road between Superior Junction and Fort William, with all the vast works connected with it, including the great elevators which the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company have constructed at Fort William. The proposition is entirely indefensible, and I think the country will not approve of it when an opportunity is given them to express their opinion.

I am not going to enter into the legal phases of this case; I should get lost if I tried it; for when the lawyers themselves disagree, a layman would get hopelessly muddled in the argument. But I do say that any business man reading this [DOT] section will say that there was provision for the settlement of difficulties as to construction, not only during the progress of the work, but as to completion as well. The question whether the road is " completed " or not, is simply a question whether it is completed under the agreement. On that we have a difference of opinion. I contend the road is not completed under the agreement. The Prime Minister takes a different view from that which, in his absence, was presented to the House the other day; If it were simply a lease for temporary operation by the Government of this branch line in connection with the through line, I do not know that I should object. But we were told the other day, or the House was led to believe, that the expropriation was to be used as a weapon against the Grand Trunk Pacific to compel them to do certain things. That is the wrong attitude in which to approach the company on this great question; for this is not a small question, but one affecting the whole nation. The Minister of Railways to-day rather gives intimation that it is the intention of the Government to buy this road.
No, I said it was not in the interest of the country. I want to treat my hon. friend fairly, and I hope he will accept what I say.

I am going to put my own construction on what the hon. minister said. I am not changing his statement, but only giving what I infer from his statement. The Minister of Railways says that it would be in the interests of the country if the Government owned this branch line as well as the through line; I infer, therefore, that he is in favour of purchasing it. According to my understanding of what the Solicitor General has said, this proposed legislation gives the Government the power to do what the Minister of Railways says it would be a good thing to do. This would seem to embrace a much larger pow*r than that referred to by my right hon. friend, which includes merely the operation by the Government for a time of the whole line, including that branch line. The investment of perhaps $30,000,000 in the purchase of this line, and of an enormous sum in the taking over of terminals, certainly should not be made until the approval of Parliament is obtained, and some provision to this effect should be inserted in this proposed legislation.

Supposing the Grand
Trunk Pacific Railway Company would not accept a lease, and the wheat crop were ready to be carried, would it be in the interests of the country that there should be no way of overcoming that difficulty? I do not think that there will be any trouble, but if there should be when Parliament is not in session, we would have no power to take action.

The Prime Minister
rather takes the view that power to expropriate is not conferred under this Act, and if that view should prevail I would not have any objection to make. But there seems to be a possibility that the Government may exercise that power by buying out the entire line and all terminals, and investing a large amount of additional capital in this great enterprise; then they will be compelled to operate or to make some arrangement with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. If it is made clear that under this statute power to expropriate is not given, I shall have no objection to the proposed legislation, but I do seriously object if the Government is to be given power to invest another $30,000,000 or $50,000,000 in property which includes terminal elevators belonging to another company.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think it would be reasonable to suppose that, having in view the present condition of the money

markets of the world, the Government would not be very much disposed to incur an expenditure of $30,000,000 or $50,000,000 for the purpose of acquiring this line. It is not necessary to go into the question of what would have been wise in the first instance, although there is a great deal to be said in favour of the view that the line should have been owned by the Government, inasmuch as the Government owned the line from Winnipeg to Moncton. There has been a good deal of discussion in regard to the operation of the branch lines of the Intercolonial by the same company, and possibly some of those considerations might have forcible application to what has been urged here. It is not worth while to enter into a discussion of a legal question which this committee cannot settle. My hon. friend the member for St. John city (Mr. Pugsley), whose opinion on any legal subject is entitled to a great deal of respect, has expressed an opinion, but we are not advised that the view which he has expressed is correct. I would point out to him that one cannot afford to be too sure of these things. I have no doubt that my hon. friend was equally cocksure with regard to the effect of the implementing clause; but the Privy Council told him that he was wrong.
I venture to say that my hon. friend will not find anywhere an expression of opinion on my part contrary to the judgment of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend was a member of the Government of that day.
Not when the contract was entered into.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, but when the contract was being acted on, and when the Government put the case before the Privy Council for decision. It is with some surprise that I learn that the hon. gentleman differed from his colleagues in his view of what that contract meant. If that is what he intends to convey, I was never aware of it before. The late Administration were very sure of their ground, but they found that they were mistaken, and their mistake has cost the country a great many millions of dollars. We want to avoid mistakes of that kind, so far as possible; therefore we do not profess to be so cocksure on these questions of legal construction as my hon. friend the member for St. John City professes to be. What the Government desires is that the Grand Trunk Pacific
Railway Company shall fulfil the conditions of the contract and statutes made and passed in 1903-4. We have urged and will urge that upon them, and I have no reason to believe at the present time that any serious controversy will arise. If any controversy does arise, we will endeavour to come to Parliament with any proposals that the public interest demand. After all, there is very little of this legislation that was not contained in the legislation of last year, which provided for the operation of this road by the Governmeent until the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company 'should accept a lease and undertake its operation. That Act was passed without dissent, and we are now asking that in case it should become necessary to operate the road during any such period as has been suggested, we should also have power to make suitable arrangements for the operation by the Government of the branch line from Lake Superior Junction to Fort William.
You are asking much more than that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What else?
To acquire.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
To lease, or
otherwise acquire. I have not yet had impressed upon me the detriment to the public interest which would result from that.
The hon. member for St. John City has alluded to the interests of the Maritime Provinces. I suppose those interests would appeal to me as much as they would to him, and I fail to see why the interests of the maritime provinces would not be thoroughly safeguarded if the Government should also acquire the line from Lake Superior Junction to Fort William. In what way would 'the public interest of any part of this country be detrimentally affected by the carrying out of even that proposal? We have not that proposal in mind; we desire simply to make provision for temporary operation of the whole eastern division, including this branch line, until the Grand Trunk Pacific, under the terms of its contract and agreement shall accept the lease and take over the operation of the road. We think this legislation is necessary because it would be manifestly to the utter detriment of the public interest thait a road upon which nearly $200,000,000 has been expended should remain idle for any considerable period of time after it is clearly capable of operation in the interest of the public. That is all that we desire; to

guard against that is all that this legislation is intended for.

But we want to know exactly what is meant. We were told a moment ago by the Minister of Railways - and it is repeated by the Prime Minister -that the object of this legislation is simply to enable the Government to operate the road pending the negotiation with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company or the Government's taking over the operation. If that be the object, we know where we are. But what I point out to my hon. friend is tihat he is asking much more than this power to operate; he is asking the power to acquire. If the object of the legislation is simply to permit an agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company providing for the operation of the road pending the settlement of their difficulty, this Bill may be sufficient. But if the ultimate object -I will not use the word " concealed," but I might-is to permit tlhe Government to acquire the road permanently under the plea that it would be better for the country to do so, then this Bill would be insufficient. In the first place, we might say that the object is to have a temporary arrangement for the leasing of the road for a limited period. There would be no question of coming back to Parliament for ratification in that case. But if the object be to acquire the road and acquire it permanently, then I contend that this ought to be supplemented by the necessity of the Government coming to Parliament for ratification of such an agreement. That is a question not of policy but of how this statute is to be drafted.

As I read this Bill and as I have listened to the remarks upon it and the various explanations that have been given regarding it, I can only conclude that it is a Bill to ask Parliament to give the Government authority to do as it pleases in regard to a matter of the highest and greatest importance to the welfare of this country. I do not think that the circumstances are such that it would be to the benefit of the country that that authority should be given. I do not think it is in the best interests of the country that the authority has been asked. If the explanation given by the Prime Minister a few moments ago is correct, tlhe Bill is then most unfortunately worded. If the intention was that this Bill should give the Government power to operate the road to lake Superior until a permanent arrangement

is made with the Grand Trunk Pacific to operate it, the Bill should have said so. But it says the direct opposite, it provides absolutely for the leasing of the branch or that it be otherwise acquired. And, as has been fully and very definitely explained to us by the Solicitor General, that meant the right to expropriate. He went on to speak of expropriating the lease as well as expropriating the road, so there can be no question whatever as to the explanation given to us by the Solicitor General.

Expropriate what
lease?

He said we are taking
power so that if there is a lease we can expropriate that lease as well as expropriate the road.

I imagine that applies
to terminals.

What ever it applies to I remember he used those words. Therefore the explanation given us by the Solicitor General is that the intention of the Government is to take power to own this road if it so pleases, whereas the explanation given by the Prime Minister is that that is not the intention of the Government, but merely that the Government shall have authority to operate the road during a certain intervening period.

You will admit that
if we are to run the balance of the road from Moncton to Winnipeg we should not be in a position that we could not run to Fort William, especially when the wheat is being moved.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We are perfectly willing to meet the wishes of my right hon. friend. We have no such ulterior motive as he seems to have in his mind, and we are willing to make it clear that if we should acquire the road by purchase or expropriation we must come back to Parliament.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I suppose my
right hon. friend's idea is that the word " expenditure " might include the purchase price of the road.

The word
" acquire " certainly means purchase.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It would depend not on that, but on the word "expenditure" in subsection 7. I suppose my hon. friend's argument is that under subsection 4 we

might acquire and under subsection 7 we might pay. We did not intend that, and I am willing to make that plain.
Why not leave out the expression " or by other means acquire " ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would be
willing to make the change suggested by my hon. friend, and to say plainly that if we do anything 'else we must come back to Parliament.

I had in mind the query of the Prime Minister as to what public interest is going to be affected by the action the Government proposes to take. In the present condition of finances throughout the world, where immense amounts of money have been invested in various enterprises, any legislation that has in it an element of uncertainty as to its ultimate effect, which interferes in any direct or indirect manner with any such enterprise, must have a serious and detrimental effect on the financial situation generally, but more particularly on that particular enterprise. If it is the intention of the Government of Canada to take over this road, even in the manner proposed by the Prime Minister, it still remains the intention of the Government of Canada to take over the operation of the line of railway between Winnipeg and lake Superior, to take that portion out of the hands of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. No such declaration can be made, no such statement can go forward, without having a most seriously detrimental effect upon the securities of the Grand Trunk Pacific, because it is thoroughly known that the successful operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific system depends in large measure upon the control by that company of its outlet to lake Superior by reason of its ownership of the terminals and of the line, and of its arrangement for traffic over the part of the lime that belongs do the Government. So I say that when we put on our statute-book legislation which, even as amended by the Prime Minister, declares the exclusion of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company from the operation of that section of their system, ox of their system and ours, we thereby discredit their enterprise; and by interfering with the successful operation of that enterprise we discredit it not only with those who have invested their money in it but with investors in Canadian securities generally. Because if this Government of Canada and this Parliament of Canada are able and minded to so interfere with tire operations of one 135
great enterprise in Canada so they may be minded at some other time or on some other occasion to interfere with some other great enterprise in Canada. I submit that this is a feature of the case that should be given greater consideration than it has been given up to the present time.
I repeat for the purpose of emphasizing it, that the whole Grand Trunk Pacific Railway system, from the Red river to the Pacific ocean, depends fo~ '* G successful operation upon the control by that system of the outlet to lake Superior.
How could they get through without running over the Transcontinental?

And this Government proposes to put legislation through this House to give the Government authority to exclude the Grand Trunk Pacific from the operation of that section of the road. In answer to my hon. friend's question, " how can the Grand Trunk Pacific get to lake Superior without running over the Transcontinental?" I agree that they cannot get to lake Superior unless they run over that road. But let me call my hon. friend's attention to the fact that an essential part of the arrangement in regard to the construction of the road from Winnipeg to Moncton is that any railroad company is entitled to claim running rights over that road, or any part of it, on terms the limitations of which are laid down in the agreement. [DOT]
That was only in case the Grand Trunk Pacific took a lease, under the Act, to run the road.
I quite appreciate that.

Then there would be
no dispute. If they take that, we are quite willing.
They have the right to take that under the Act of 1903-4. The Act gives them the power to take temporarily the completed portions.
They must take the bitter with the sweet.

I am not learned in the
law and am not prepared to give an opinion as to this or that section, but I know and everybody knows that it was an essential consideration put forward at the time of the passing of the Grand Trunk Pacific Act that the railway to be constructed under that Act should be for the use of any railroad company that saw fit to use it. And I say that for this Government to ignore that



fundamental principle and say: Because we have the authority to ignore it we will ignore it, would he just the same as the proposal to expropriate the property from lake Superior Junction to the lake front, and would be so considered by those who have invested their money in the enterprise and by other investors as well; and would be properly so considered. It would be an absolute breach of faith on the part of the Government in dealing with a great enterprise with which the welfare and prosperity of this country is so essentially bound up. There is no necessity at all for the terms of this Bill as it stands or as it is proposed to be amended by the Prime Minister. If the object to be achieved is merely that the Government shall have a fair opportunity to operate the Transcontinental between Winnipeg and Moncton, and needs this piece of road in order to facilitate that operation, the very foundation of the agreement between the Government and the Grand Trunk Pacific as to the operation of the Transcontinental contemplated the joint use of those tracks, in case of necessity, by more than one railway company. All that the Government requires to do is to take power to lease running rights from the Grand Trunk Pacific or, if you like, to take power to expropriate running rights over that road so that they would have the same opportunity as the Grand Trunk Pacific itself of using those tracks to get to the lake front for such business as they have to handle.

Suppose the
Grand Trunk Pacific w%s not operating the Superior Junction branch at all and that it became necessary for the Crown to operate the road from Winnipeg to the head of the lakes. Does not this give them that power?
Mr. OLIVER. Certainly. But the suggestion I have made also gives them the same opportunity, and does not interfere with the Grand Trunk's continuing the operation that it is now carrying on.

This does not interfere
with their present operation.

Yes, it does. If I read
the English language correctly this gives the Government the right to acquire, and if it gives them the right to acquire it also gives them the right to exclude the company from whom it acquires that right. It gives the Government the right to ex-
[ilr. Oliver. ]
elude the Grand 'Trunk Pacific from the profitable and useful operation of this branch line, which is their property, and from the profitable and useful operation of the road between Lake Superior Junction and Winnipeg. It is against this evident intention to exclude the Grand Trunk Pacific from that operation that I protest most. I have no fault to find with the Government for undertaking to operate the Transcontinental between Winnipeg and Quebec during the intermediate period. I have no fault to find with the Government for taking authority to expropriate, if they like, those rights and to operate this branch jointly with the Grand Trunk Pacific. But I take every objection to this Government's taking such action as will exclude the Grand Trunk Pacific	from	the
profitable operation of the line	between lake Superior and Fort William, which is the Grand Trunk Pacific's own property. I can only repeat that it is an interference with the operation of a great railway system upon whose successful operation depends in a largo measure tin. welfare and prosperity of our whffle western country. I cannot think that the Government is well informed in undertaking to put such legislation on the statute book.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think my h >n. friend is unnecessarily alarmed. The Government is just as anxious to preserve the stability of Grand Trunk Pacific securities and the credit of the country generally as the hon. gentleman or anybody else could possibly be. We shall havp all those considerations thoroughly in mind in connection with any arrangements that we make with the company. Further than that, we have given very careful consideration to the interests of the western provinces of Canada with which this railway system is so closely concerned, arid the House may be assured that in any arrangements we may make we shall have the most careful regard for the interests of those provinces.

No one supposes that the Government has any sinister intention against the company; far from it. But the fact pointed out by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), that this legislation may have the effect of injuriously affecting the credit of the Grand Trunk Pacific securities, and the arguments that he has brought forward in support of his contention, are certainly entitled to some consideration. It seems to

me that there is great force in the views he has presented and in the manner in which he has presented them. If this Bill were simply to say that the Government, pending negotiations with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, shall have power to operate the road, there would be no objection at all. But unfortunately the language which was used the other day led one to believe that there was something beyond that. We have the word of the Solicitor General that the Government wanted a weapon-and he used the word two or three times-when they came to deal with the company. Now, if the Government want a weapon, it is because they want to compel the company to do something it does not want to 'do. Again, the Government is seeking not only power to operate the road, but power to lease the road permanently or temporarily.
My right hon. friend has submitted an amendment which does not altogether satisfy me. I have one which I shall submit to him and which, if it does not prove acceptable, he can take into consideration. I would suggest that a further clause be added to the Bill to the following effect:
Any contract for a permanent lease of the said line, or the acquisition of the same, shall be subject to the ratification of Parliament.
If there is a contract providing only for a temporary arrangement, there is no necessity for coming to Parliament; but if it is in the nature of a permanent acquisition, I think it should be submitted to Parliament for ratification.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is no objection to the idea of ratification by Parliament. But the expression " a permanent lease " is not a legal expression, nor do I know precisely what construction would be placed upon it.

If you had a
lease for fifty years it would be a permanent lease.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Suppose it were for ten years? I would like to know just what that means. If my right Ihon. friend will send it to me I will consider it.
Say a lease pending the completion of the line.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If my right hon. friend will send his amendment to me I will endeavour to work it out.
At one o'clock, the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock. 135i

In reference to the Bill that we were discussing when the House rose, I beg to move:
That the Bill be amended by adding thereto subsection 8, as follows:
8. Any contract for the lease of the said Lake Superior branch for a term of four or five years or for the acquisition of the same shall be subject to the ratification of Parliament.
That meets my views.

The amendment as worded still leaves the idea that the Grand Trunk Pacific is to be excluded from the operation of this branch. I think that the purpose of the Government would be served quite as well if such words were used as would not seem to exclude or would not be intended to exclude the Grand Trunk Pacific from the operation of the branch. I would urge that the operation be one of joint operation instead of one of exclusive operation as against the present proprietor of the road.

That would be covered by the conditions of the lease. I have been comparing this section with other similar sections, and I think it is in terms such as are used in' cases of that kind. I think the expression "lease or acquire" will meet the idea that the hon. member has in mind.
That will be entirely satisfactory to me, but I would like to have a word from the Minister of Railways or from the Prime Minister that that was what the Government had in mind.

If we wanted to block the Grand Trunk Pacific from going down to lake Superior, we could do so, because we could make unreasonable terms and block the company in many ways; but that is not the desire of the Government. We want to work in harmony with the Grand Trunk Pacific in order to get business.
You want their business in the West?
Yes.
This amendment suits me.

Amendment agreed to.
Bill reported as amended and amendments concurred in.
The House again in committee on Bill No. 110, to amend the Dominion Elections Act-Mr. Doherty; Mr. Sevigny in the Chair.
On section 4-hours of polling extended -8 a.m. to 6 p.m.:

I beg to move:
That this Bill be amended by adding as section 1 the following, and by changing the numbering of section 1 and the following sections accordingly:
1. Section 70 of the Dominion Elections Act, chapter 6 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, is amended by adding thereto the following subsection :
"(h) Any person during the time he is a director of or holds, either directly or indireotly, a controlling interest in any incorporated company having a contract or agreement, expressed or implied, or any unsatisfied claim arising therefrom, with or for or against the Government of Canada on behalf of the Crown, or with or for or against any of the officers of the Government of Canada for which any public money of Canada is to be paid."
Clause (d) of section 70 of the Dominion Elections Act says:
Every person directly or indirectly, alone or with any other person, by himself or by interposition of any trustee or third party, holding or enjoying, undertaking or executing any contract or agreement expressed or implied with or for the Government of Canada on behalf of the Crown, or with or for any of the officers of the Government of Canada, for which any public money of Canada is to be paid, during the time he is so holding, or enjoying, undertaking^ or executing.
When this Act was passed, business was not carried on as extensively by means of joint stock companies as it is now. This Act was passed for the purpose of securing as much as possible the independence of candidates from the Administration of the day. There is an Act on the statute-book to secure the independence of members of the Senate and of this House; but a person, by putting his business in the form of an corporated company and getting a few nominal directors appointed, although he still owns the majority of the stock, can contract with and sell extensively to the Government, as has been done since the beginning of this war. If a private person cannot have a contract expressed or implied with the Government for the smallest amount, why should a person who holds the majority of the stock of a company and who gets big contracts from the Government, be eligible as a candidate for membership in this House? If we want to secure the independence of the candidate, _ we must amend the Act in the way which I have indicated by my amendment. I presented a Bill to this House some time ago to amend the Act respecting the Senate and the House of Commons, and I hope it will become law later on;

but the first requisite will be to secure the independence of the candidate.
I have taken advantage of the Bill presented by the minister to move as an amendment my Bill to amend the Dominion Elections Act. I hope the Government will accept my amendment. It is only fair, I think-especially at this time when the Government is purchasing, sometimes without tender, such great supplies of goods-that the independence of candidates, as well as the public interest, should be protected T do not wish to dilate on this matter; the amendment speaks for itself.

I have great pleasure in supporting the amendment. Unless we are to wipe out the Independence of Parliament Act altogether, I think this amendment is desirable. A leading shareholder in an incorporated company, that has a contract with the Government, may be in exactly the same position to all intents and purposes, iso far as his interest is concerned, as if that 'contract were with him individually.

The amendment
as proposed operates against any director.

I understand it is
against any shareholder holding a controlling interest.

And any director also.
There are in this House, and have been ever since 1867, many men who are directors of companies having contracts with the Government. The hon. gentleman surely does not intend it to apply against all these men?

If he is a director of the company, I think he should be regarded as the same as one having a controlling interest. The fact of his being a director implies that he has something to do with the management of the company.
Take the case of the Senate and the banks.
But this applies to one who is a candidate only.

It is a singular provision that under the Independence of Parliament Act the disqualification applies if the company has a contract for the construction of a public work. I do not know that this is generally known for it is a well-known fact that there are members of this Parliament who are large shareholders in, officers of, and, in at least one case, I believe, president of companies which have contracts '

with the Government for the construction of public works. It is a singular thing that when Parliament passed the Independence of Parliament Act it provided that shareholders in companies having ordinary contracts with the Government should not be disqualified, but that this should not apply to shareholders of companies having contracts for the construction of public works. To-day a member of this House who is a shareholder in an incorporated company having a contract for the construction of a public work is disqualified, while a senator who is in that position is liable to a penalty of $200 a day. Yet we know there are gentlemen in this House and in the Senate- at least such is my information-who are in that position.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
What is the
position?
Senator Curry is one.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I was not asking for the names, but what is the position?

If a man is a shareholder in a company having a contract for the construction of a public work he is disqualified from holding a seat in this House, or if he sits in the Senate he is liable to a penalty of $200 a day. In my own constituency, the firm of Rhodes, Curry & Company, of which, I believe, Senator Curry, a most worthy man, an honour to the whole country, is president, has a contract in my own constituency for the erection of a post office involving a sum of perhaps $300,000 or $400,000. I do not suppose he is aware of the fact that there is such a provision in the statute. It is certainly anomalous.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What statute?

The Independence of
Parliament Act.
