The effect of the proposed amendment would be very far-reaching. My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), for instance, is director of a newspaper. I do not know that it is very profitable. If that newspaper gets a little advertising from the Government, that would disqualify him for being a candidate.

That would not be a
contract for the construction of a public work.
No, but I speak of the effect of the proposed amendment.

But suppose the hon. gentleman owned the newspaper in his own right, his position probably would not be very different from what it is-I am assuming that he owns the company; but of course, he can speak for himself as to that. I call attention to section 19 of the Act:
This Act shall not extend to disqualify any person as a member of the House of Commons by reason of his being,-
(a) a shareholder in any incorporated company having a contract or agreement with the Government of Canada, except any company which undertakes a contract for the building of any public work.
Now, with regard to the Senate, section 20 provides:
If any person, who is a member of the Senate, knowingly and wilfully becomes a party to or concerned in any such contract, he shall forfeit the sum of two hundred dollars for each and every day during which he continues to be such party or so concerned.
Then, subsection 4:
This section shall not render any senator liable for such penalties, by reason of this being a shareholder in any incorporated company, having a contract or agreement with the Government of Canada, except any company which undertakes a contract for the building of any public work.
I do not suppose that ten per cent of the people-I venture to say, not ten par cent of the members of this House or of the (Senate-are aware of that exception. I am sure that the gentlemen whom I suppose we all have in mind, and who occupy high positions, would not knowingly do anything contrary to the law. But I am confident that unwittingly they are violating the law.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think that was inserted in the statute when the Canadian Pacific railway was first in contemplation, with a view to preventing any person interested in that company being a member of Parliament.
But it is made general in its application.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, but I think that was the occasion of it.

I think the amendment of my hon. friend from Prescott ought to carry, or else we ought to amend the Act in another particular and make it uniform. It seems absurd, for instance, that a man like my hon. friend from Colchester (Mr. Stanfield) whose company might have a contract for hundreds of thousands of dollars for supplies-

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: All through now.

Then, the hon. gentleman can take a more disinterested view. I say it is absurd that the company of which a member of Parliament is a member should be disqualified because his company has a contract for $10,000, $20,000 or $100,000 to build a public work, yet he would not be disqualified if the contract were for supplying the Government with lumber or any kind of material, even though the amount might be very much greater.
I think we should make the statute uniform ; either adopt the amendment of my hon. friend, or strike out the whole section. I think it would be wise to adopt the amendment; certainly such a provision is desirable in the case of a shareholder who has a large, substantial or controlling interest in the company.
Would you make it apply to every director?
I do not see why not.
Many of us are directors representing absent shareholders in an old company; it is merely a nominal position.

A director usually has large interests in the company; even if he has not a controlling interest, he may be induced to come, to Parliament to act in the interests of his company. I do not want to reach the ordinary shareholder by this legislation, but I think that a company in which a member of Parliament has a controlling interest should be debarred from contracting with the Government, and that if such company does contract with the Government, no director or person having a controlling interest in it should be enabled to become a member of this House. In the Bill which I presented to amend the Senate, and House of Commons Act, I added to the exception respecting the building of a public work, the following:
And except any company of which he is a director or in which he holds, directly or indirectly, a controlling interest.
I hope that the Government will adopt this Bill after they have accepted the amendment which I have proposed to the Dominion Elections Act. I agree with the hon. member for St. John city that if the Government do not want to accept my amendment, they should wipe out the section at present on the statute book with respect to the standing of a person who is interested in a company which undertakes a contract

for the building of a public work. There is not as great danger of abuse in permitting a company in which a member of the Senate or of the House of Commons is a shareholder to contract with the Government for a public work, because most of these contracts are obtained by calling for tenders, whilst many ordinary contracts are obtained without calling for tenders, as was the case during the first months of the war. I think the hon. member for Colchester can corroborate what I have said in this respect; he was concerned in a large contract with the Government.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: And gave good value, too.

I do not doubt it, but I think that all persons should be on an equal footing. If the Government would like to have a certain man as candidate in a certain county, they might offer a large con-, tract to the company of which he is a shareholder, and the candidate might make enough out of that contract to pay his election expenses. If elected, he would not he independent; he would be tied to the Government. The law which is on the statute book to-day was passed to prevent this, but it does not go far enough, and,the object of the proposed amendment is to secure the independence of members of the House of Commons and of the Senate.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The company of which I am president, and which bears my own name-a company of which I am proud- during last year sold goods to the Militia Department. The first order was given while I was in England, and I knew nothing about it until I arrived home. If this Bill becomes law, I as president of that company cannot be a candidate for election to the House of Commons, and I have several good friends on the other side of the House who would be very sorry not to see me here. Any amendment of this kind would apply to the hon. member for Northumberland, N.B. (Mr. Loggie); his company sold goods to the late Government, and if his party returns to power he will expect to do a little more business with the Government.
I appeal to the good judgment of the committee, therefore, not to pass this proposed amendment; perhaps the law could be amended in some other way that would be just as good. .

If the Government had received as good velue from all the contractors as they received from the

hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Stanfield), we would be' in a better condition than we are at the present time. I am sure that my hon. friend gave good value, but unfore tunately the same cannot be said of all contractors. But these arguments are not to the point. I am one of those who would be very sorry not to see my hon. friend in the House; if the Tories are successful in electing a candidate in Colchester, I do not want to see any other Tdry than my hon. friend; but I hope that a Grit will be in his place next time. The law of the independence of Parliament is a very strict one: men have been disqualified here, because unknowingly and unwittingly, they had a contract with the Government which was a mere bagatelle. I remember the case of Mr. Harry Corby, who in 1891 found that he was disqualified to sit in the House because, unknown to himself, he had been a contractor with the Government. In this country, as in England, the law of the independence of Parliament has been very strictly carried out. The hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx) very properly says that if a man can be disqualified for having with the Government a contract which is a mere bagatelle, surely a man who has a controlling interest in a large company ought to be disqualified also.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The proposal of the hon member for Prescott has certain merits which the committee ought to consider very carefully. The extreme oase which be very properly puts before the committee is where a man who is interested in a certain business which: he has been carrying on in his own name sees fit to incorporate himself, as it were, and to change his status in that way. The hon. member very properly argues that contracts between such a company and the Government are very much the same as contracts between the Government and the person who thus puts himself in the form of an incorporated company. But there is something to be said for the other side of the case. Eveiy one realizes that during the past twenty-five or thirty years there has been a tendency more and more to carry on the business of the country by means of incorporated companies. The best business ability and the best enterprise of the country are frequently represented by persons who have considerable interest in such companies and who, on account of their ability, may be selected to be members of the board of directors.
The question would be whether or not it is desirable in the public interest that all persons of that type and possessing that interest, which might not be a very great one, in an incorporated company, should be excluded from representing the people in this House, ot from becoming members of the Senate. I think that side of the case would demand the consideration of Parliament; and therefore I would suggest that the amendment be .allowed to stand until it has received a little more attention on the part of the Minister of Justice and his colleagues in the Government, and that we should proceed in the meantime to consider the other sections of the Bill.

I think it is my duty to call attention to a case that happened in my own experience. One of my opponents was nominated against me while he had a contract with the Intercolonial. I produced the contract to the returning officer and filed a protest. But I was put to the whole trouble of an election campaign while the man had a running contract with the Intercolonial Railway for the supply of ties. I think there should be something in the law that when a man is actually a contractor and the contract can be produced, some means should be taken to prevent that man from being nominated. In my case there seemed to be a loophole of some kind, and we had all the trouble of a campaign, although the man was not competent to be elected.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No doubt it would be desirable if that matter .could be determined then .and there. But the difficulty that would arise is that in order to obtain that end the returning officer would have to be empowered to determine the question whether a man nominated was a qualified candidate. There might be such absolutely simple cases as the hon. gentleman suggests, but in many cases the determination of the eligibility of a candidate would involve very considerable investigating.
Might not an oath be required of the candidate that he was qualified to be a candidate? Fot instance, if he were .a postmaster he would not be able to take the oath.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That suggestion, no
doubt, .has merit; but I would point out that an affidavit by .any person that he was a qualified candidate would involve his swearing not only to questions of fact but to questions of law. If he simply

swore to his interpretation of the law he could mot be convicted of perjury. Of counse, if, all of the causes for disqualification were iset out dm the affidavit and he had to swear only to questions of fact, then if he made a misstatement -in his affidavit he could be subsequently proceeded against for perjury.
I think in the New Brunswick statute -they have such -a provision.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Has the hon. member for Prescott looked up legislation in other countries to isee if there is any of the character which he proposes?

No, I have not searched the legislation of -any other country; but it struck -me that if the purpose of the Act was to secure the independence of members of this House and of the Senate, and of all candidates, as business is carried on nowadays very largely by means of companies, we should make some effort to reach those who control -an interest in any -company having a contract with the Government.

I suppose the object of the Independence of Parliament Act. is to make it secure that any dealing a member may have with -the Government will not influence him -as a member of the House. Under -modern conditions it is possible that the -entire Act should be revised. As has been pointed out, the business of the country is largely carried on by companies. Men -group themselves together instead of -acting singly as in year-s gone by. If this suggestion were carried out to its ultimate conclusion it would exclude ' every man who is a director o-r owns a large number of shares in a company. This would exclude some of the very best men in Canada from taking -any part in public life. Ten men would be excluded under present business conditions to one who was excluded under former -conditions when business was carried on individually. Let us take an example. My hon. friend fom Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) was -mentioned. There -are others who -are in the same position. The reading room would not be complete without certain newspapers; that is admitted by every person; yet not a single copy of a newspaper could be subscribed for if the proprietor of that paper or a man holding stock in the company happened to sit in the House. Now, that is not the intention of this legislation. That would be absurd.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: These things are so complex that it is difficult to get legislation that will accomplish the object.

Yes, without going to
absurd lengths. The question is of such magnitude that it cannot be decided in an hour or two. It should be considered very maturely, not for an hour, but perhaps for a year, in order to find out how present conditions may be met by legislation that will be up to date; for certainly the old legislation does not apply to present conditions.

If my hon. friend objects very much to the directors being reached, I can forego that portion of the Bill and include the words " one who has a controlling interest" so as to prevent a man from evading the law by putting his business in the form of a company.

I think that could be
very easily got around. I am not taking strong ground one way or the other. I am simply pointing out that the matter is far more complex than might appear on the surface. As to directors, it is a well known fact that many men are willing to put a large amount of money in a certain business, provided John Smith will become a director. There are many men who will take stock in a company if a certain man in whom they have confidence is made a director. This director might only hold one share, or just what was sufficient to qualify him as a director. This legislation would exclude that director from being a member of this House, although the only interest he had in the business was his salary and this one share.
A man might hold 49 per cent of the stock of a company and sell goods to the Government, while the man who held 51 per cent could not sell the Government a box of matches.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It occurred to
me while the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) was speaking that there might be a good many cases that this would not cover. For instance, the general manager of an important company might be paid partly by salary, and partly by a percentage of the profits. That man would he just as directly interested in the company as any one of the directors, perhaps much more so, and yet the legislation of my hon. friend would permit him to be a member of Parliament, while a director having an insignificant interest in the company could not become a member of Parliament.
I suppose that the general manager is nearly always a director too.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not always.

We can add the words
" general manager, secretary, or any officer or employee of the company."

Would my hon. friend define what he means by controlling interest? Is that defined in his amendment? I know of companies in Montreal where the controlling power is held by one man who apparently does not own more than one or two shares; but nothing can be done in that company without his consent and participation. What they do is to nominate their employees to be shareholders or directors of the company. These employees hold the shares, but their employers of course have the controlling power. How are you going to get over that difficulty? I agree with the hon. member for South Renfrew that it is a very complex question and one that eannot properly be discussed across the floor of the House. I think it should be debated in a small committee. Before deciding what should be done I think we should examine the legislation of other countries. This question must have come .up in England for instance, but I am not aware that in England anybody who -is a member of a company or a shareholder or even a director cannot be a member of the House of Commons. I am aware that when such a man becomes a minister, the Prime Minister, generally speaking, asks him to resign his directorate or whatever position he holds in the company. That would lead me to believe that in England, where they have a very good system as every one will admit, even the director of a company is not prevented from becoming a member of Parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I understand that in the United States in connection with the larger corporations, such as railway companies, they have had in recent years a system that is called a voting trust, whereby certain persons accept the beneficial ownership in the shares upon condition that the voting power shall reside elsewhere. It would not be a very difficult thing to apply a system of that kind to companies in this or any other country. Then you would have the result that persons having not the beneficial interest, but the voting power, could be members of Parliament, while persons having the beneficial
interest but no voting power would be excluded from Parliament; and that would defeat the object which the hon. member for Prescott has in view and which I agree is a very laudable object. All these considerations seem to indicate, as the hon. member for South Renfrew has said, that this is not a matter to be disposed of hastily. It should receive very careful consideration, and, as my colleague the Postmaster General (Mr. Casgrain) has said, we should also examine any legislation on the same subject in other countries enjoying similar institutions.

The Ontario Legislature amended their Act a few years ago to exclude certain classes of business, and they limited the amendment. I forget the details, but an amendment of that kind was passed some years ago.

I should like to ask if, after all, it is really a crime to be a member of Parliament or to be engaged in business? From the trend of the discussion that has taken place, it would almost seem that there was a crime more or less concealed in one or the other of these vocations. Unfortunately in this country almost everybody is engaged in business. We have no class of people who are altogether dissociated from business, and can give their time and attention solely to political affairs. We are a country of men engaged in active business life, and a very large majority of our people are struggling with difficulties. But we have to take the country as we find it, and it is from these people that we have to pick the men whc will manage our political affairs. Are we going to pass legislation that will render that practically impossible? I take it that the first essential is that, for service in a legislative capacity, we should get the most capable men that the country affords. While I quite agree that there must be restrictions, I submit that it is not in the interests of the country in any degree to prevent the best brain we have and the highest character and the greatest experience, from entering the field of public service in a legislative capacity.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As this Bill is the product of the committee, I may say that we had before us a very large number of suggested amendments to the Dominion Elections Act. I think that, without at all minimizing the importance of this suggestion many of those were more important and more pressing than this present suggested amendment can be. After giving these dif-

ferent matters our consideration, I think I will speak correctly on behalf of the committee when I say that in view of the many things that might properly be dealt with in the Dominion Elections Act, and in view of the fact that what seemed to us more urgent and more pressing was that we should get better machinery to enforce the law than we have, we rather reached the conclusion only to suggest the few simple things in regard to the Dominion Elections Act which we have submitted and to look to Parliament tliis session, at all events, for an improvement in the law mainly in the direction of improving the machinery for enforcing the law we have. I quite agree in what has been said about the necessity of careful consideration being given to the present suggested amendment. Its effects might be very far-reaching and you might reach one class of people and allow to escape another class of people against whom the very same argument might be made. I notice that this proposed amendment is limited to people who have a controlling interest. If I understand it correctly this amendment was introduced for the purpose of making the law consistent, the argument being that, inasmuch as we deal with the individual and exclude him if he has a contract, we ought to exclude people who are interested in companies which have contracts and who are directors or who have the controlling interest. In many companies you may have shareholders who have by no means a controlling interest, but who might have their entire fortune invested in the stocks of these companies. A man in that position has his all at stake in that company and it seems to me that he has just as direct an interest-perhaps more direct an interest-than the man who may have the controlling interest, but who also may have other interests and other sources of income. At first glance it would appear to me that if it is desirable to do this we ought to draw the line somewhere else than between the man who has fifty-one per cent of the shares and the man who has only forty-nine per cent of the shares. If it is desirable it ought to go further. As to its desirability, I must confess that there is room for a little reflection and I think there is no pressing necessity at the present time for dealing with this question in the manner in which it would have to be dealt with under the circum stances.

I thought we might have an election before another session, and I

thought this was an opportune time to present this amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Great foresight.
If I withdraw this amendment will the Government promise that there will be no election?

I understand this matter will be allowed to stand for the present. Speaking with regard to the question of requiring an affidavit of qualification, and with regard to the objection raised by my hon. friend from Bonaventure
4 p.m. (Mr. Marcil) who cites a case wherein he says it is quite a grievance, I find that I was right as to the province of New Brunswick. If the qualification of any candidate is questioned, it must he done on or before two o'clock of the day of opening the election, and the sheriff shall give the candidate or his agent, or some one of the persons signing his nomination paper, immediate notice thereof, and unless the necessary declaration of qualification, as in the form (H) in the schedule, is made by the candidate or an elector for him before the sheriff, and filed with the sheriff by two o'clock of that day, he shall not enter his name in the general poll-book.
That would in all probability meet the difficulty which my hon. friend from Bonaventure referred to.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think the question was ever raised in New Brunswick.
Yes, I have known a declaration to be required. I know that in the case of one of the postmasters who was disqualified the objection was raised.

I see a provision in the Ontario Election Act that no person shall be ineligible as member of the Assembly-
By reason of his being a surety or contractor or liable for the payment of money for or on account of the maintenance or tuition of an inmate or pupil of any Government institution ;
By reason of his being a postmaster elsewhere than in a city, town or incorporated village, or interested in a contract for carrying the mail between two or more post offices neither of which is in a city, town or incorporated village or of his being the surety of any such postmaster or contractor;
By reason of his being a surety for a public officer or Ontario land surveyor or other person required by the law to furnish security to the Crown.	[DOT]

But there is also this provision:
A person elected a member of the Assembly, who is at the time of his election a surety as aforesaid, shall, before he sits or votes therein take and complete such action as may be requisite to relieve him from any thereafter accruing liability in respect of his suretyship, and no person who is liable as such surety in respect of any accruing matter shall sit or vote in the Assembly.
If a person were elected tto this House, and there was a disability or disqualification existing, he would have to remove this disqualification before taking his seat.
On the question being put: Shall the amendment be agreed to?
I understood it was to stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is nothing else in the Bill to stand. I do not want to unduly press the matter, but if the committee were ready to deal with it now there would be some advantage in doing so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did suggest that it should stand for consideration, and I am perfectly willing that it should stand if my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laur-ier) thinks it desirable. Since the discussion has taken place, and particularly in view of some of the considerations which my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has put forward as to the complexity of the question and the difficulty of determining it in so short a time, I would be perfectly willing to have it dealt with now, but on the other hand I do not object to have it stand. -

If the Government is not going to accept the amendment there is no use of pressing it, and we might as well dispose of it now. My hon. friend (Mr. Proulx) knows that if the Government does not accept it, there is no use of pressing it.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This Bill stood for further consideration of sections 4, 5 and 10. The questions that arose with regard to sections 4 and 5 are practically the same. Section 4 prescribes the form of the petition and wlhat shall be required to be contained in the petition protesting the election, and section 5 makes similar provision for the form and what shall be required to be contained in the counter petition. The matter, with regard to which there was some difference of opinion in connection with these two clauses and which gave rise to a desire that they should stand, was that the petition contained in them required that the petitioner should give such particulars as might be necessary to prevent surprise or unnecessary expense to the respondent and insure a fair and effectual trial. Objections were made to the sections as they were proposed; and although we have not been able to have a complete meeting of the committee which submitted the Bill, those of us who could gather together have considered the objections and endeavoured to find a course to meet them. I am afraid I cannot say that we are quite agreed as to the proper method of meeting the objections. I would like to suggest this as being an improvement and, it would seem to me, going far enough to obviate the inconveniences that it was suggested might result from this requirement. If I understood it rightly, the objection most insisted upon to the requirement was the difficulty of defining just what would be covered by such particulars as are necessary to prevent surprise and insure a fair and effectual trial, and more particularly the difficult posi-

tion that might be created, if the parties, in the absence of special provision for obtaining further particulars or otherwise modifying. the petition, found themselves in a situation where the question of the sufficiency of the particulars would arise only at the trial. To obviate that, I think these two provisions should be amended so as to provide in substance, that within a limited delay-I would suggest five days after the service of the petition-either of the parties might make application to the judge to summarily determine the sufficiency or insufficiency of the particulars set forth in the petition. And in the event of finding the particulars insufficient, the judge should have power to order such further particulars as he might prescribe and if the judge arrives at the conclusion that the particulars in the petition are not sufficient, the furtner particulars that he prescribes shall be furnished within a further delay of five days from the making of his order. In that way you have a delay, at the outside, of ten days from the service of the petition.

Sections 4 and 5
of this Bill present many difficulties. If it were possible to frame an amendment to attain the end which the committee had in mind, "and which the Minister of Justice also has in mind, I am sure it would meet with the approval of the House. But I must confess that upon reflection, I see objections to section 4, and difficulties in its language, which did not strike me as forcibly when we were considering the Bill in , committee as they do now in view of the criticisms that have been made. Perhaps it would be well that the committee should understand clearly just what the purpose and effect of section 4 of the Bill is. Let me call attention to section 11 of the Controverted Elections Act as it is now on the statute book:
The petition presented under this Act may he in any prescribed form; but, if or in so far as no form is prescribed, it need not be in any particular form, but it must complain of the undue election or return of a member, or that no return has been made, or that a double return has been made, or of matter contained in any special return made, or of some such unlawful act as aforesaid by a candidate not returned, and it must be signed by the petitioner, or all the petitioners if there are more than one.
Under the practice that has grown up in the trial of petitions under the Controverted Elections Act, the petitioners make general charges against the respondent, and as was stated by the Minister of Justice, the petition recites the

language of the several prohibitory sections of the Dominion Election Act-those sections which make certain acts corrupt acts. This is open to objection. It is unfair, in a certain sense, that the petitioner may file a petition charging the respondent with the violation of every section of the Elections Act, though, .perhaps, he has at the time no evidence of the actual violation of these provisions. Further, it is obviously irritating to the respondent and to his friends to be charged with the violation of practically every feature of the Elections Act when possibly the petitioner had in. mind only the violation of one or two sections. These are the objections to section 11 of the Act which the committee had in mind when it attempted to modify the same, and it was to overcome these that section 4 of the Rill was drafted. Let me read section 4:
4. Section 11 is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
" 11. The petition presented under this Act may be in form " A " in the schedule to this Act. It must complain of the undue election or return of a member, or that no return has been made, or that a double return has been made or of matter contained in any special return made, or of some unlawful or corrupt act or acts, and shall contain such particulars of the complaint set out in the petition as may he necessary to prevent surprise or unnecessary expense to the respondent and to insure a fair and effectual trial; and it must he signed by the petitioner, or all the petitioners if there are more than one.
Thus, the amendment requires that the petition shall contain particulars of the complaint, whereas under the present section of the Act the complaint is set forth in general terms only. Now the word " particulars " in the law respecting election trials has a meaning that has been fixed by the rules of the election courts in Canada and in England. It is well to know what " particular " means, 'and how comprehensive the term is according to the decisions of the courts. The draftsman of section 4 used in the latter part of it the phraseology of the definition of particulars under the Controverted Elections Act as contained in the English petition rules. Rule 6 is as follows :
Evidence need not be stated in the petition, but the court or a judge may order such particulars as may be necessary to prevent surprise and unnecessary expense and to insure a fair and effectual trial in the same way as in ordinary proceedings in the Court of Common Pleas, and upon such terms as to costs and otherwise as may be ordered.
Therefore we have incorporated in section 4 the English definition of particulars,
according to the rules followed in controverted election cases in England. Hon. gentlemen know that particulars in election cases aTe exceedingly minute and definite. I have in my hand a textbook on the English Corrupt and Illegal Practices Prevention Acts, by Jelf, and, in a form to be used in the giving of particulars, I find that the following particulars are required where the plaintiff alleges payment of expenses by the respondent: number of particulars, charge, date, name of voter, registered number of voter, district, particulars, by whom alleged to have been paid, and so on. It will he seen, therefore, that in Canadian election courts, as in England, "particulars" has a certain significance as a well-settled term, and if we pass clause four as it is, its effect will be that the petitioner will be required to put in his petition the smallest details in connection with the several complaints which are made. I do not think that the committee had this in mind, and in that view I think I shall in this be supported by the Minister of Justice, the hon. member for Calgary and the hon. member for Carleton, New Brunswick. We had in mind the formulating of some enactment which would compel the granting of more particulars than are required by section II of the Act, but I do not think it was the intention of members of the committee that we should go so far as to say that the petition	should	contain	particulars	which,as	understood	in	practice	wouldbe practically pleading evidence. I think the members of the committee will all agree that it was never intended that we should in our election petitions plead particulars, as is done in controverted election cases. A person might decide at the last	moment	to	file	a	petition,	and itwould hardly	be	fair	to	require that evidence should be pleaded, or that the complaint should set forth all particulars. I am afraid that if that were the case, the Act would become almost a greater nullity than it is to-day. The trial of an election petition is not like the trial of an ordinary issue in court. The jurisdiction to try election cases, as was pointed out the other night, originally rested with Parliament, and that jurisdiction was handed over to the courts. The trial of an election petition, therefore, is more in the nature of an inquiry or investigation, and I think that it would be hardly proper to insist upon particulars in the petition. I am of the opinion that it would be better to drop this section, and either restore the old section or make
it perfectly clear that it is not intended that tlhe petitioner must set forth what is really evidence. If there is any amendment which we could frame which would make that sure, I- should be content. The hon. member for Calgary suggested to me privately to-day that his sense of that section is that the petitioner may allege that in a certain district the respondent or his agent committed certain offences at certain times. While it is possible to give it that interpretation, it is extremely doubtful whether that is the whole scope of the section. I am sorry that I do not see my way clear just at the moment to accept this section as it is; I am afraid that it does not express what was really the intention of the committee.
What was the intention of the committee?
The intention of the committee was, in some .way or other, to compel the giving of further particulars than are now required, but it was not the intention to require the pleading of evidence.
Wlbat objection is there to leaving the present provision as it is, which gives the judge power to order particulars?
I am rather of opinion that it would be bettter to restore the old section. It would create less difficulty than might arise from an attempt to amend it, for the time being at least.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The objection to the
provision as it stands now is that whereas you require a man to file his petition within forty days, you allow him to do that by a document that conveys no idea to the respondent of what the grounds are upon which he is attacked. What he does know is simply that an election petition has been filed against him. Then, as it works out in practice, the petitioner is enabled, under the present proceedings for the furnishing of particulars, to make his real case six months or perhaps a year later, after he has endeavoured to find out whether he had any reason at all for filing a petition. To me that seems radically unfair. I quite agree with the hon. member for Halifax that the committee did not have in mind that we should require particulars in the sense that we should require the name of every man who may have done an act, and so on, but I am disposed to insist, so far as I reasonably may, upon this section, or upon such modification of it as may meet the serious objection which has

been suggested by the hon. gentleman; because I think that this is the one section of this Bill that seeks to remedy a present condition in the law which is very unfair to the respondent. The other provisions of this Bill all tend to deprive the respondent of means of defence available to him under the present law, means of defence which we think he ought to be deprived of, because they lead to great delay, which delay ultimately operates to defeat the practical operation of the law. But we felt that we were the more justified in depriving the respondent of these means of thwarting the petition that the present law now gives to him, if we did at the same time remedy that law where it seemed to us to be unfair to him. The result of that view of this Bill would be that if these clauses be dropped, then our Bill would be one that would operate entirely to further facilitate the petitioner, to place the respondent in a more difficult position. That seems to be unfair to the respondent. Speaking for myself individually, I would almost feel that if we cannot pass these clauses, or something analogous to or approaching them, something more closely attaining the idea of the committee, as the hon. member for Halifax expressed it to have been, then perhaps the whole Bill ought to be dropped. I realize the force of what the hon. member for Halifax has said with regard to the possible interpretation that may be put upon the word "particular," as used in this section, by reason of the established practice regarding the requirement of particulars; and the section will overshoot the mark, I am prepared to admit, if it should be interpreted as requiring in a petition all these things which in practice appear to be required in a bill of particulars. If I correctly apprehend the present condition of jurisprudence, the courts in effect require every detail of each particular act committed, including the individuals who were parties to it, either as bribers or as bribees, or in any other capacity. It occurred to me, while the hon. member for Halifax was speaking, that possibly we might obviate that better if we adopted some form of expression that would not involve the use of the word "particulars," and at the same time would require something more specific in the setting forth of the grounds alleged in the petition. I tried to put this into words, and it seems to me that possibly the objection raised by the hon. member for Halifax might be met if, instead of demanding, as the section now does, such particulars of the complaints set out in the petition as may be necessary to prevent

surprise and unnecessary expense on the respondent, and insure a fair and effectual trial, we should say:
And shall specify the grounds of such complaint sufficiently in detail to prevent surprise or unnecessary expense to the respondent and to insure a fair and effectual trial.

Will it be possible to specify grounds of complaint in such a way as to afford no assistance whatever to the respondent? Is there any way of specifying the grounds of complaint, other than in the usual way of furnishing particulars, which will he of any use to him? That is the gist of the whole question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am disposed to think that one might have considered that the furnishing of particulars did not require as minute details as appear to be required, in practice at all events, in the giving of a bill of particulars. What struck me in the argument of the hon. member for Halifax was that as we are using the word " particulars " and requiring particulars there may be serious ground to apprehend, as he suggested, that the courts may take that up and say: Well, that now means precisely what we have been holding to be required in a bill of particulars; it is the very same word. It seems to me that we would obviate that argument anyway, our requirements would be something else than that. I do not pretend now to be able to define just what extent of specification would attain the desired end. We have to put upon the courts the burden of determining what degree of particularity would be necessary. I think we sufficiently indicate that we do not mean to require a bill of particulars in the petition, and we would have to leave the courts to determine what degree of specification would be sufficient to prevent surprise.

I have not had the privilege of listening to the discussion so far this afternoon, but it does seem to me that the Minister of Justice has described things exactly as they occurred in the committee. The committee certainly did not intend to recommend words to the House which would entirely obviate the necessity of going to a judge and demanding particulars, as is done under the present practice of the courts; we specifically did nothing to repeal the section. The practice regarding particulars is established by the rules of the courts, and I presume is pretty well known all over Canada. The rules
are- provided for under sections 85 and 86. I remember that I suggested in the committee that we should put in the word "general " between the words " such " and " particulars " in the tenth line. If I remember correctly, it was the understandjng of the committee that we should take somewhat the same position as is taken in regard to a statement of claim in an ordinary suit in court. That is, you must acquaint the respondent generally with the case you are bringing against him, so that he may be in a position to file a general answer. If further particulars are required the present rules allow a respondent to apply for them and get them. Personally, I think the suggestion made by the minister is a good one. There would then be no necessity for using the word "particulars" which has a legal meaning at the present time. Like the minister, I cannot say how the court would interpret the word " particulars ". I certainly think that a respondent should have a pretty general knowledge of the complaint that is being made against him. I am anxious to see the Bill go through, knd personally I have not very much fault to find with what the minister has suggested.

I also want to see the
Bill go through, but if we enact the provision which requires the particulars to form a part of the petition, then if the judge should be of the opinion that the particulars are not sufficient the whole petition would go by the board, and the whole proceeding would be void. Why not leave the present section as it is, and provide for a further time, say five or ten days after the service, in which the particulars can be furnished? Then you do not make the particulars an essential part of the petition. What I am afraid of is that if the judge decided the particulars were not sufficient he would simply dismiss the petition. The minister says that it is unfair to allow a petitioner to get information after he has decided to file a petition, but I am not quite sure whether that is reasonable. The man who buys votes does not do it openly; he goes quietly and in secret to the men whom he wants to influence, and makes an arrangement with them. As a rule, it is not until two or three weeks or a month after the election is over that the information begins to leak out which will enable the petitioner and his agents to support the petition. We should not be too strict in reference to the petition. If the respondent is guilty of a corrupt act, you are doing no

injustice if you allow the petitioner a reasonable opportunity of establishing these corrupt acts. I think we had better leave the section as to petitions just as it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps the suggestion of the hon. member might meet what is required, but we should have to make it imperative that the particulars should be given within the time. If we go back to the old provision and require a petitioner to give particulars within five or six days, we shall not be very much improving what the Bill does. It would mean that he would have five or six days longer to give particulars in, than he would have under the Bill as now drafted. If the suggestion of the hon. member would bring about the same results as the provision in its present form, I should be disposed to accept it. I do not know what the views of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr, A. K. Maclean) are on the subject.
I am satisfied with the Bill as it is.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: So am I.~

The object of this Bill is to expedite the trial of petitions. The defendant must.be informed as to what he has to answer to. If you do not put that in the petition, you have to give it at a subsequent time. If the particulars are not in the petition, the defendant is entitled to move for them and that means delay. Therefore, I say that the petition should contain everything that the defendant has to answer to. If the petition contains only general terms, so that the defendant cannot prepare a proper defence, that means more delay. I am satisfied with the Bill as it is drafted.

I notice that the Bill is satisfactory to the leaders of both parties. It is also satisfactory to me, with this exception:	If you confine the petitioner to
forty days within which he must give particulars of the offences which he intends to prove, you will have mighty few petitions. My observation has led me to believe that particulars cannot be obtained in forty days, especially as regards the large outlying districts, such as the constituency of Nipissing or any constituency in Ontario or Quebec that is spread over a large area. As the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) has said, you have to delve to get the particulars on which a petitioner bases his right to an action. I firmly believe that if particulars have to be given, the filing of

petitions will be greatly curtailed; and, so far as my reading of criticisms of the Elections Act goes, that is not what the public desire.
They desire that when the petition is filed it shall be tried out, and not traded off against some other petition. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice put in the Bill a clause which says that the judge shall go on. I objected to that because, unless you provide some proper means for the judge going on after the petitioner or respondent has abandoned the case, the word "shall" is inoperative. Unless you provide some means through a public prosecutor, or some other means of procuring the evidence in order that the trial may go on, the provision will be found inoperative. By limiting the time to forty days for the giving of all particulars upon which the petitioner relies you will do away with the filing of petitions altogether.

If the time were lengthened from forty days to sixty days the petitioner would then have more opportunity of looking for particulars.
On section 4-form of petition:

Before this passes, I want to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Justice to the fact that in the committee there was some discussion about form A. If the minister will read over form A he will come to the conclusion that it does not cover the real intention of the committee. I think he will find that the form goes very much farther than the section does. The form mentioned would compel the petitioner to give all the particulars and it would render practically nugatory any provision which might exist for the furnishing of further particulars. Form A contains the following:
Here state the grounds on which the petitioner relies, and, in case illegal or corrupt acts are alleged, the particulars of each of such acts are prescribed by section 11.	[DOT]
I would like the minister to consider that for a moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman's objection be met by striking out the word "each?"	-	.
That would go a long way towards it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: "The particulars of each of such acts."
I very much prefer the suggestion which came from the minister a few moments ago to change the section and change the form to correspond with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Personally I like the
Bill as it was originally drafted. I have been trying to meet the suggestions that have been made, but if we could have agreed upon the Bill as originally drafted I would have preferred it to stand in that way. But I do think that if the section is to be passed as it is drafted, we should add to it something in the nature of what I mentioned at the opening of this discussion this afternoon. I think that we should make provision which would entail a very brief delay but which will afford an opportunity for the determination of the question of the sufficiency or insufficiency of the particulars and one further very brief delay for the petitioner to complete these particulars if they are found insufficient.
That might cover it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would move to amend section 11 by adding as subsection 2 the following:

I suggest that, instead of a further delay of five days, you leavi it in the discretion of the judgs.

As a matter of fact, in the practice of any person, have election petitions been delayed for want of particulars? speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If preliminary objections and delays are all wiped out and there are no longer the means of getting delays, then people will reach out to find what other means there are and we will have this question of particulars if we leave it open. We will come back to the preliminary objections and people will be 136
fighting about particulars for months unless we tie it down to a definite time.

The petitioner might find on the thirty-ninth day that there were certain particulars which were necessary to validate his petition and it might be physically impossible to get these within the succeeding five days. Why should not the judge be given a discretion in the matter just as you do in any other court of procedure where you ask for an enlargement and where the question is left in the discretion of the judge? Why not do the same thing in this case? I think that, as in all other civil cases, it might be left to the discretion of the judge to determine whether or not a longer term than five days should be given. In bringing on an action for trial, if you do not serve your notice within the specified time, you have the right to make a summary application to the judge to go on. If there is no surprise, no prejudice to the other party, it is allowed. Why should you not do just the same in the case of a petitioner who is furnishing particulars in support of his petition?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In an ordinary proceeding you are dealing with a fight between two individuals about their own affairs and if they choose to delay indefinitely nobody is hurt. Here we are legislating to correct an evil which is an evil from the public point of view and that is the undue dragging out of election proceedings. If we are going to leave it in the hands of the parties we will get no correction. It is in the hands of the parties now and the result is that these proceedings 'do not go forward at all.

Would the minister be willing to substitute the word "shall" for the word "may" after the words "given in the petition and"? What I would like made clear is that the judge shall not dismiss the petition because he thinks the particulars are insufficient. The amendment would then read as follows:

That would mean that the judge cannot dismiss the petition, but must make an order for particulars. That would meet any objection I have.

On section 10-examination of witnesses.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This section gave rise to considerable discussion. It was suggested, among other things, that to some extent it overlapped section 45. I beg to move:
That section 10 be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
Subsection 1 of section 45 is repealed and the following is substituted therefor:
" If at any time after the presentation of an election petition it is made to appear to the court or the trial judges that any witness intends to leave Canada and cannot attend the trial of an election petition, or that for any other reason it is desirable in the interests of justice that the examination of a witness be proceeded with forthwith, then an application to the court on notice to the parties to the petition, the court may grant an order for the examination of such witness at a time and place and before a person to be named in such order, and the witness may thereupon be examined touching the matter
[Mr. Pugsley.j
complained of in the petition, due notice of such time and place being given to the parties to the petition, who may, by their respective counsel, attend such examination, and examine and crossexamine such witness; and such examination shall be reduced to writing and signed by such witness, and when duly returned by the examiner, and purporting to be certified by the examiner, may be used by either party to the petition on the trial thereof."
The only changes in the Act made by this amendment are the following: first, it is made clear that the application for the examination of a witness may be made at any time after the presentation of the petition, instead of, as at present, only after issue is joined or at the trial; second, that the application may be granted not only when the witness is absent from Canada, or may be absent from Canada, but when from any other cause it is made to appear to the judge that in the interest of justice the witness should be examined forthwith; third, that whereas under section 10 as proposed the application for examination might be made ex parte, under the amendment, the application will be on notice to the other party.

Amendment agreed to.

Mr. Chairman, before the vote is taken on this item, L wish to make a few remarks concerning the expenditure since 19X2 on those protection works at Laprairie. During the session of
1911-	12, $15,750 were voted, this amount being seven-twelfths of the full $27,000 which had been placed in the Estimates by the late Government. Thait vote was frittered away on work by the day during the summer of 1912. During the session of
1912-	13, $45,000 were appropriated to the same purpose, namely, the carrying on those improvements during the recess of 1913. In the month of August, 1913, tenders were called for in 38 newspapers of the province of Quebec. That goes to show that the Department of Public Works was not remiss in advertising for (tenders towards carrying on those works. Three tenders were put in, one by Mr. E. J. Rainboth, for $70,051.60; another iby H. Duranceau and N. Poupart for $72,676.73, and still another by F. C. Jackson for $110,326.23. The minister did not award the contract to the lowest tenderer. Why was that? His reply to my question during the session of 1914 was that Mr. Rainboth was not in a position to meet the wishes of the Department of Public Works, who wanted 1,400 feet of that road to be completed immediately-I should explain that these 1,400 feet had to be completed during the fall of 1913, so as to connect that piece of road with the King Edward boulevard. The minister stated that as Mr, Rainboth was unable to comply with the request of the department and build those 1,400 feet of road immediately, while the next lowest tenderer was ready to go on, he, Mr. Rainboth, on that account, asked leave to withdraw his tender. That was a scheme for the purpose of putting aside Rainboth, and entering later into a private agreement with Duranceau and Poupart. Now, what are the actual facts as they come out to-day? Have Messrs. Duranceau and Pouparlt signed their contract? No, Mr. Chairman. Have they constructed that piece of road, as requested of Mr. Rainboth, by the minister? No, Mr. Chairman, I know that every one in Laprairie and Napierville would have been glad if that piece of road had been completed in the fall of 1913. Unfortunately, we have been deceived; the second lowest tenderers could not carry on the works any more than Mr. Rainboth could have done himself. N'ow, the Minister of

Public Works will allaw me to inquire whether he has a letter dated the 23rd of October, 1913, from Hon. Mr. Caron, Minister of Public Roads for the province of Quebec, in which it is pointed out that the Dominion Government has still a good deal of work (to do on that piece of road which is in the extension of the King Edward boulevard; that nothing has been done during the summer and that the writer could not see how that piece of road could be opened in the spring of 1914. Was it not further stated in that letter of Hon. Mr. Caron that the Provincial Government would complete its part of the work in a couple of weeks if the temperature proved favourable. The Provincial Government spent a good deal of money on that road, and is anxious that (the whole road should be ready by next spring, so that it may be an attraction for American tourists, and a convenience for the farmers of the South shore, whom it will enable to proceed to Montreal at all times of the year. In that same letter, the Hon. Mr. Caron made the proposal to the Minister of Public Works that he, Mr. Caron should have the whole road built himself, according to the Estimates of his own engineer for the district of Montreal. The Provincial Minister further stated that he was in a position to construct the dam, the raising of the road with earth and the rip-rap revetment on each side, and complete the whole by the end of June, 1914. And lastly, he put himself at the minister's disposal to make arrangements to determine the cosit of this piece of road. How was this offer received by the Minister of Public Works? The reply was in effect that the letter of the 21st of the same month (1913) had been duly received, which dealt with the construction of the King Edward boulevard in the parish of Laprairie; that the department had only lately invited tenders for the work and that there was at the time before Council, a recommendation to award the contract; that the contractor agreed to do the work by the ensuing fall; that, were it not that so much had already been done with a view to let out the' contract, the minister would hhve been pleased to discuss the matter with Mr. Caron.

Poupart and Duranceau had signed their contract for $72,678.73, the

Will you believe it, Mr. Chairman, after a year and a haAf, that work has not made any progress. And what is the cause? Patronage, pure and simple. Why was the contract not awarded to the lowest tenderer? Mr. Rainboth is a distinguished civil engineer, well acquainted with that kind of work, while Messrs. The protection wall which was to be twelve inches thick and bound together with cement, was built of dry stone, field or cobble stone, without any binding; after it was completed, a thin coat of cement was spread over it. Then came the autumn rains of 1914; from night to night some part of the wall crumbled to the ground, sometimes over a length of five hundred, six hundred and even fifteen hundred feet; the farmer and passers-by used to say that the Germans had crept up during the night and effectively bombarded the wall. I am quite aware that the minister and his friends, in order to shield themselves, will put the blame on the district engineer. I am quite aware that some Conservative politicians demanded the dismissal of Mr. Michaud, the district engineer, and put
their foot to his throat to prevent him from doing his duty. Those Tories were in no way backward in crying out: Our turn has come to rule; the Liberals have no more anything to do; and as for you, Mr. Michaud, you toe the mark or you will lose your position. Mr. Michaud, as I stated before, should have performed his duty, and even take his dismissal if the Government had gone that far. Very likely we would not see that which now is going on at iLa-prairie. I now wish to take up the subject of the temporary road. How much has the Department of Public Works paid for this temporary road at Laprairie?
(Translation): $4,000.

I may say to the minister that that work could be done for $300. If he paid $4,000 for it he paid just $3,700 too much.
(Translation): I will ask the minister if he intends to make a temporary road this spring and whether if would not be better instead of making a temporary road to make a good macadamized road with a small wooden bridge. That temporary road which has cost the Government $4,000, has not cost the contractors $300; I assert that fact in all sincerity, and the engineer who has recommended the expenditure deserves to be superannuated and given a pension.
I wonder how long such a course will he pursued in respect of public works in our constituencies and how long the people will be deprived of the improvements which ought to be made with the moneys wasted for party ends. I am familiar with what has taken place in my county and the same things holds good for other parts. Work is undertaken, not for the benefit of the people, but in contemplation of election results. I will ask the minister how much will be required to complete the works? I am informed that the department intends to widen the road and make the wall 36 feet instead of 24. I have not a great deal

It is true that they have not carried out their contract as well as we would have liked and that some delay has taken place and some difficulties have arisen. Mr. Paradis, the engineer in charge, has given the matter a great deal of consideration and he has had difficulties in respect to the engineering problems, just as the contractors have had in respect to their contracts. My hon. friend mentioned the fact that we spent $4,000 for a temporary road last year to make conditions passable there, and he complains that this amount has been altogether too extravagant. That is the statement of my hon. friend; but "as against that, with all due respect to him, I may say that in the opinion of the engineers of my department this amount of $4,000 was very well spent and was cheap for the work that we secured for the purpose of making the temporary road. I am giving my hon. friend the report of the engineers of the department, who have had an opportunity of examining the work. In respect to the width of the road which my hon. friend has referred to, I may say that the road as at present laid out is only 24 feet wide, and I do not think it would be possible to change it at present. We are anxious to get the road completed as quickly as we can, and I quite agree that we must have a temporary road that will be satisfactory to the travelling public for the coming year. This will be taken up at once by the department,

and I am satisfied we will be able to pro vide a temporary road immediately that will meet with the requirements of the public that travel from Montreal. I do not know that it will be possible to build a macadamized road as the hon. gentleman suggests, but we will make a road of a temporary character that will be entirely satisfactory and will proceed with the contract as fast as we can. I am going to have a very thorough investigation made of this particular work, because I recognize its importance; and if it turns out that the present contractors are not carrying on the contract in the workmanlike manner they should, I will be prepared to recommend that it be taken out of their hands and to see that the work is built under the direction of the officers of the department, with a view of having it completed at the earliest possible moment. I understand from the minister's answer Ithat the contract was not awarded at the Bulk sum of $72 ,000, but at so much a yard. The contractors receive $1.50 per yard for the revetment wall. This road is not in my constituency, but I have had a little experience of it. Apparently the river remaining at the high level is washing in the banks to some extent. I have not heard much about the sanitary conditions or any objection in connection with that side of the question.

Having reference to the sanitary conditions by reason of the curtain in the lock gates, if that be the correct expression, there is always a splendid opportunity for drainage; at all events in the spring the whole river flows right out.

But you inflict very serious damage if you open the locks and let the water rush out. It affects the bank of the river through the city of Winnipeg and people complain very bitterly about that condition. We have to exercise great care in opening the locks in that way so that the water will go down at a very gradual speed.

If the river only falls gradually it will not flush the undesirable element out very satisfactorily?
The river has to be flushed out at a very slow rate.

flushing, it is not doing very much. Everybody in the West is interested in the city ol Winnipeg. I would like to say that there is liable to be serious consequences from emptying the sewage of Winnipeg into that water, made dead water, by the dam at the locks. There must be a very serious sanitaiy problem involved which ought to receive attention before the terrible results that might occur have occurred. At some time, if there is a terrible outbreak of disease in the city of Winnipeg, the people will be very much interested and it will take very stringent measures to remedy the condition. I think the time to apply the remedy is before the catastrophe occurs. When we know that there is a condition which in the nature of things must tend to very undesirable results.

In this connection I wish to draw the minister's attention to the fact that for a number of years there has been before the Government application for assistance or action looking to the protection of the river bank in front of the city of Edmonton. In many respects the two conditions are similar. The city of Edmonton is located along the river bank; and if the bank falls away the ground supporting the buildings also falls away and the streets and buildings in the city are destroyed. About 500 yards of the river bank, in front of a very thickly inhabited part of the city, where the main street runs close to the edge of the bank, has fallen away so much that some houses and a part of what at one time was the main street have sunk into the valley. The damage occurs from time 137
to time. Very many representations have been made to the Government asking for assistance in protecting the bank, and several surveys have been made by the department. I think delegations have come here urging the Government to take means to protect the bank; and there has been a suggestion that if the Government would make the plans, the city would be willing to put up half the cost to show its good faith and willingness to help itself. The conditions are so different from what they are at Prince Albert, the bank of the river being 200 feet high at Edmonton, that it is absolutely beyond the financial ability of the city to protect the property interests on its own account. At the same time we feel that the Government has the same responsibility in regard to the protection of the bank at the front of the city of Edmonton as it has in regard to the front of the city of Prince Albert. If the minister has any information he can give in regard to the intentions of the Government towards Edmonton, I shall be very glad to have it.

I have some knowledge
of the conditions at Edmonton which my hon. friend has described. In regard to the small item in the Estimates for Prince Albert, it is not altogether fdr the protection of the bank; it is for the protection of the wharf and probably of the bank to some extent at the same time. The two cases are probably not parallel; but I fancy the case in the city of Edmonton is parallel to some extent to the case we have in the city of Winnipeg in respect to the outflow of the water through the St. Andrew's lock, causing a great deal of damage to the banks as to which very serious complaint is made from time to time by the owners of lots on the river. This complaint has always been transmitted from the city council to the Government, and we are held blamable to that extent. In view of the fact that no new or special items of any account are in the Estimates for this year, nothing has been suggested in the way of providing protection for the banks either in Winnipeg or in Edmonton; but I believe when we are here next year, we shall have to get together and see if we cannot got Parliament to vote an amount for each place with a view of protecting the banks at both cities. The work in both Winnipeg and Edmonton is very necessary, and it probably belongs to this Parliament to render certain assistance. The city of Winnipeg, like the city of Edmcnton, is very



willing to contribute its share; but it does not deem it its duty to pay the whole cost of protection of its banks. This matter will come up at a later date.

Several surveys of the bank at Edmonton have been made by officers of the Government. The problem is possibly complicated or difficult; and, while I would not wish to throw any aspersions on the abilities of any officers who have already made examinations, I think the Government would be acting wisely if it secured the best talent that could be got on this continent to make an expert examination of the ground with the information that the surveyors have already collected.
The gentlemen who have made the surveys are no doubt expert engineers, but I doubt if they have any expert knowledge of the peculiar conditions which have resulted in that sliding bank. If there are any parties who have expert knowledge of these conditions, I would urge upon the Government the desirability of getting their advice, based on an examination on the ground and with the advantage of the surveys that have actually been made, so that when Parliament meets again the Government would have that information before it on which to base any consideration it might see fit to give to the matter.

I will have that looked into.
Sturgeon river improvements, $9,500.

This is a matter in regard to which I have had some correspondence with the department. In that correspondence I said that while I had no doubt the Government had the best intentions in entering upon these improvements, they apparently have incurred the opposition of a number of the settlers wlho occupy lands along this river. I would urge upon the minister that however desirable it may be to constitute this large creek or small river into a measurably navigable stream, there are certain property rights of the people owning the land on both sides of the stream that are entitled to be regarded. Apparently, the officers of the Government, in dealing with the matter, have proceeded without any regard to these rights, having torn down fences and blown up bridges which were, as I understand it, actually on the property of these owners, and built at their expense and for their convenience. In the first place, I do not think the Government had the right to do this, and if it had the right,

I do not think they should have done it, at any rate without due consideration, or without compensation to the people so injuriously affected. I do not know how far the minister is aware of these facts, but I have taken some trouble to bring them to the attention of the department by correspondence, and I take this opportunity of bringing them to the minister's own notice.

The matter is an important one, evidently. However, I must confess I do not remember having had it under my personal observation. But I shall be glad to make a personal matter of it and to look into the facts. If conditions are as my hon. friend suggests, they should be corrected, and will be corrected.

I cannot help but say,
from the information I have received, that the officers of the Government have acted very reprehensibly in ignoring what was thoroughly understood to be the absolute property rights of the people who owned the land along the stream. I have no fault to find if the Government sees fit to spend the money to make this stream navigable for motor-boats,-that is the most that can be hoped for. The stream will make a pleasant connection between two lakes, and it runs through a nice tract of country. I have nothing but commendation for the Government for undertaking this work, but in carrying it out they have certainly run counter to the rights of the people occupying the land and have incurred a great deal of enmity. I am not saying that I am particularly sorry for that.
We shall have to correct that.

I should like to see it
corrected.
Harbours and rivers, B.C.-Fraser river improvements, $300,000.

navigation between Westminster and the gulf of Georgia?

improvements, $15,000.

To remove obstructions
to navigation on the Upper Fraser, Nechaco, Stuart and Tachi rivers which drain a large area tributary to the Grand Trunk Pacific

When such plans as the

A gentleman in British
Columbia has done me the honour of asking me to bring to the attention of the minister a matter relating to a wharf at Kootenay bay, in the riding represented by the hon. member for Kootenay. He says that although this engineer told him that he would recommend the same wharf as his predecessor had recommended, as a matter of fact he recommended a floating wharf, pile-protected, which would cost about $5,000. There actually has been constructed only a comparatively inexpensive floating wharf, which, the writer complains, is not adequate for the business, and is not in accordance with the understanding had with the Government. A wharf costing a large
sum of money did not appear to be necessary; only one man was very specially interested in it, and it was thought that a floating wharf would be sufficient. In view of the fact that, on the recommendation of the engineer, we have carried out the construction of that floating wharf instead of a wharf costing $7,500. A few days ago I asked the Minister of Public Works to give me some information with regard to dredging plants purchased by the department in the

In the last year some very useful and necessary dredging was being done at a place called Little Bras d'Or, opening up a channel which makes a proper entrance in to the Bras d'Or lakes.
