There is a material reduction here: it is $300,000 less than last year.
Is it intended to do that work or will the item merely stand in the Estimates?
The dredging is generally all done, the vote is usually exhausted.

The dredging I am interested in is in the Restigouche river. Some $30,000 has been spent at that mouth of that river around the property of the Bay de Chaleur Mill Company. I do not know whether the minister intends to continue that work. It is merely adding to the value of private property. I have heard former Ministers of Public Works advocate more dredging in Bonaventure and Gaspe; but they always told us that the dredges were very scarce but would come in the future. I have heard that promise for the last fourteen or fifteen years. Very little dredging has been done in that 'district. In the Baie de Chaleur they build breakwaters and wharves, but very few of them can be reached by a steamer. Some of them might be made very useful if dredging were done by the department. The chief engineer, who is very familiar with the district, could inform the minister where some very useful dredging could be done. At the Bonaventure river, which is the outlet for important timber limits, dredging was started in 1908 or 1909, but the dredge was taken away before the work was completed. A breakwater was built to keep open the mouth of the river at the entrance to the harbour, and the idea was to dredge out the entrance so that boats could go in and load at the wharf. The work was not completed. The dredge, which was owned by Mr. Lemoine, was removed to another place. Some useful dredging could also be done at Maria, where a wharf has been made and at New Richmond and Ruisseau Leblanc and other places on the coast. The minister would be well advised to have his officers report to him the work that might be done in that respect. Mr. Tache, district engineer for Bonaventure, is an experienced official who used to be on the north shore. He is familiar with all the conditions in the Baie de Chaleur. I am sorry to say that although the late Mr. [DOT]Monk, when Minister of Public Works, asked Mr. Tache to report fully on all the works required there, and I understand

that Mr. Tache did so. The Department of Public Works carried out but very few of his recommendations. If economy has not been practised generally throughout the Dominion in public works it has been in Bonaventure. We have only two items this year, one for $1,500 at Paspebiac and one for $2,000 at New 'Carlisle on a coast line of 1,500 miles where people live largely by fishing and have a hard time to get along. Many works which have been commenced on the coast have remained uncompleted. I do not want to give the list because I might frighten the Minister of Public Works, but seeing that the constituency has this long - shore line, with a wharf or breakwater about every ten miles. Only about four or five of these wharves are accessible to steamers. The others are practically only commenced. An extension would make these wharves much more useful to the fishermen, and to the people of the locality generally. As the minister knows, practically only the fringe of the Gaspe peninsula has been touched so far. The interior of the country has not been opened up to navigation at all. It is an immense pulp country, and a great country for agriculture, though the season is shorter than in the rest of the province of Quebec. The fisheries in the Baie des Chaleurs are about as good as any in Eastern Canada. Railway communication is very poor, but now the Minister of Railways has his law on the Statute Book, I hope he will remedy this state of affairs. I know the Minister of Public Works is a progressive man, and I hope he will do something for the Gaspe peninsula too. I do not expect to get anything to-night, but I am just doing a little proselytizing. 1 want to call his attention to the fact that at Chandler, in the township of Pabos, in the county of Gaspe, quite close to Bonaventure, a large pulp industry has been established. Unfortunately it is the case that it sometimes takes Americans to realize the value of some of the resources of this country. A syndicate from Philadelphia has opened up this pulp business with a capitalization of between two and three million dollars, and in the spot which was a wilderness five or six, years ago there is now a thriving town, with all 10 p.m. that is necessary to give employment to the people. This syndicate is going to utilize the Gaspe railway, and the deep water wharf that the department has constructed at Gaspe basin, and they intend to carry on a large business. I want to point out to the minister that if the department extended proper
facilities, industries of this kind of work could be started all along the coast. We not only want wharves extended, but some dredging done, so that the boats can get in and out all along the coast. I hope the minister will pardon me for having gone into this matter at such length, and I hope that at the next session of Parliament he will remember Gaspe peninsula, which has been overlooked this year.

I am quite sure that my hon. friend will appreciate the fact that it. is very difficult for me to be familiar with the local conditions which he has so well described to us. I will promise him that I will present his statement to Mr. Dufresne, who has not yet completed his dredging plans for the coming year, and who I am sure will carefully consider what the hon.. member has said.

I notice by the Auditor General's Report of last year that several thousands of dollars were spent in the county of Rimouski, in dredging a small brook at St. Mathieu. I should like to ask the minister on whose recommendation the work was done and for whose benefit it was?
I have not the information here, but I can get it for my hon. friend.
That was for hand dredging.

The shovels are less expensive than those the Minister of Militia got. They have no holes in them. You would suppose, Mr. Chairman, that a new highway of transportation was being opened up from lake St. Simon to St. Fabien. You can almost see large merchant ships plying, between St. Mathieu and St. Fabien. I' think it will be suffiicent for me to quote, the report of the Minister of Public Works, for the year 1913-14, page 218:

St. Mathieu-Dredging.
Saint Mathieu, in the county of Rimouski, is situated four miles south of the station of St. Simon, and is an important parish with a population of about 1,500. Farming and lumbering are the principal industries of the locality. There are two saw-mills, one of the best butter factories of the district and one butter box factory.
There are, at St. Mathieu, two lakes separated by a strip of marshy land; Ithe upper or west lake is about 4 miles long, and the lower lake 1J mile. The discharge of the two lakes is what is called River St. Simon, and passes by St. Fabien, near the station of the Intercolonial railway. By dredging between the two lakes and a portion of the river, it will permit of navigation to a depth of 3 feet sufficient for the driving of logs and timber.

Very useful work.
Mr. LAPOINTE (reading);
During the fiscal year 1913-14, the strip of land between the two lakes was dredged for a length of 400 feet by a width of 30 feet, and an average depth of 4 feet, containing an area of 13,200 feet or 1,955 yards. The entrance of the river was also dredged for a length of 900 feet by a width of 35 feet, and and average depth of 4 feet, containing an area of 31,500 feet, or 4,666 cubic yards.
Amount expended, $4,804.89.
Who owns the lake?

My hon. friend the member for Richmond and Wolfe (Mr. Tobin). The Minister of Public Works has just stated that this log driving was a very useful work. Well, this is the first time I have heard of the Federal Government giving money to help the lumber operators in driving their logs. I know that under the provincial law, lumber operators have certain rights of expropriation, but they have to pay for those rights. The hon. member for Richmond and Wolfe is the owner of this lake. The timber limits in the vicinity are owned by the Trois Pistoles Pulp and Lumber Co., of which the hon. member for Richmond and Wolfe is president; and I think he can bear me witness that no lumbering is done there now. I think this was only a scheme to get money out of the treasury of Canada.
When we see in the Auditor General's Report the words " making a navigable channel from lake St. Simon to St. Fabien," we must conclude that it is a very fine title for a very small thing. I really think that this work should not have been done and that the money of the country should not have been spent there. I know that river and lake very well. I have been there on a couple of fishing trips and there is very good trout fishing. A friend of mine at Rivibre du Loup said it would be very easy

to go and fish in lake St. Mathieu. "Why?" I asked. "Because," he replied, " we can go there by motor boat from the station at St. Fabien; we have dredged the river to such an extent as to permit motoring." I do not think the department spent that money for the purpose of giving sportsmen a chance to go fishing in lake St. Mathieu but I do think there is no other purpose served.
I am always generous to hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, and especially so to Tny hon. friend ft'Om Richmond and Wolfe (Mr. Tobin).

The hon. member for
Kamouraska (Mr. E. Lapointe) said that the lake belonged to myself. I will say that it is a private lake. I have owned it for years although the lumber further up belongs to the Trois Pistoles Pulp and Lumber Company, of which I am presiuent. We have never asked for any work to bo done in that oart of the country and certainly no dredging. It was a surprise to me and my company when we were informed that there were people at work dredging that small brook. It is only a small brook that you could jump across at places,-eight or ten feet wide. No lumber is floated down it. Probably, as my hon. friend from Kamouraska said, this improvement will be very useful for fishing purposes but in the public interest it was not called for and I think the money of the country could have been spent on more profitable work than dredging this small brook which will enable you to sail down from lake St. Mathieu to St. Fabien.

Did they need
rubber boots for it? -

How much water is there
in this brook when they required rubber-boots to do the work. For shovels that cost about $8 a dozen they charged $15 a dozen. These items do not amount to very much money but the purchase of rubber boots for working in a small stream like this is simply putting the country to unnecessary expense. I do not know who asked for the work. I would like to find out from the Minister of Public Works.
I will look it up.

Will the minister
let us know who got the rubber boots?
Yes.

Is it customary for the
department to buy boots for men who are

doing work for the department and who are receiving the ordinary wages? Do they buy clothing as well?
That has been a common practice for many long years.

I understand from the
minister that Mr. Dufresne, who has charge of the dredging in his department, has not yet finished his programme?
No.

I would ask him to take into consideration the necessity of dredging the St. Lawrence opposite Three Rivers. The Grand Trunk comes in on the south side of the St. Lawrence opposite Three Rivers and the only communication between the Grand Trunk wharf at Three Rivers and that at Doucet's Landing, is by way of ferry. Last year the city of Three Rivers went to a good deal of expense in getting a modern steel steamer to perform the service between these two points. Two or three times during the summer the service was interrupted on account of boulders and shallow water. I would ask the minister to have an inquiry made a'nd see if it would not be possible to dredge this channel. It is a great inconvenience to have the boat put out of commission. The propellor is often broken by these boulders and we are without communication with the Grand Trunk sometimes three, four and five days. There is no dock where we can repair the boat except at Sorel. It takes one day each to go to Sorel, dock the boat and bring it back. It would be a very small item. Five or six days' dredging with a Government dredge would be sufficient to enable the traffic to go on uninterruptedly during the summer months and even during the winter. It is very seldom that the river freezes opposite Three Rivers during the winter but sometimes the water gets low in the winter, as it does in summer, and it would be a very material help if we could have this work done.

I will see that my hon. friend's statement is brought to the attention of Mr. Dufresne to-morrow.

This is like the other dredging ; we have not Mr. Dufresne's programme for the work ready yet. This is just for the maintenance of our own departmental dredges that we have in existence there.

When the minister gives more information I wish he would let me know the programme of dredging in the province of Saskatchewan as well. I spoke to the minister before dinner and asked for some information in regard to the price paid for the Saskatoon post office site and the amount paid and when the minister gives his answer I hope he will give it so that it will go into Hansard.

In some years past there have been river improvements on the Athabasca at Grand Rapids. There does not appear to be anything in this section of the Estimates regarding the Athabasca river. Is there any provision anywhere for the continuation of those improvements?

We have no provision made up at the present time -as the programme has not been completed for the dredging work but if there is necessity for any work in that locality it can be provided for out of this vote. I will bring the remarks of the hon. gentleman to the attention of Mr. Dufresne.

The work at Grand Rapids on the Athabasca has claimed the attention of the Government for several seasons. It is a very difficult piece of work and perhaps some mistakes may have been made in the method in which the work has been done; but it is of very great importance to carrying on the trade of the north country until the Waterways railway is completed. Therefore, I would urge upon the minister that with the opening of spring it would be right and proper that an examination should be made of the condition of the rapids and the result of the previous work, and that if there is anything that can be done to better the conditions for the business of the coming season, it should be done. There is a period of low water after ths ice goes out; that is, as soon as sprier; opens, there is low water for a short tima when work can be done to better advantayr

than it can be done at any time until the late fall of when winter sets in. My impression is that while some betterment has been created by the work done, some difficulties have also been created that it may be well to have 'removed.
We will have the matter looked into.

Grouard is a town situated on Buffalo bay, partly an arm and partly a separate lake from Lesser Slave lake. The original intention was to have the shallows, which to a certain extent separate Buffalo bay from the lake, dredged so that lake steamers could pass freely up to Grouard settlement. Now that the railroad has gone into that country and there is a railroad station at Sucker creek on the south side of the lake about ten or twelve miles from Grouard, it is just as necessary as it ever was, if the people of GrouaTd are to have the best .advantage from the nearness of the railroad, that there should be free navigation from the railroad station at Sucker creek to Grouard town on Buffalo bay, and that the shallows intervening between the bay and the lake should be dredged so that the lake steamers could pass freely. I would like to bring that very strongly to the attention of the minister.

I will take the matter up with the department.

fMr. Oliver.]

Last summer the department called for tenders, and I thought the contract had been awarded because a certain contractor from Montreal brought some machinery to Grenville, which is opposite Hawkesbury; but I was informed the other day by the minister in answer to a question that I put on the Order Paper that no contract had been awarded. How is it that the contractor came to Grenville with machinery expecting to start on the work? In fact, he urged upon the town council of Hawkesbury and the town council of Grenville to press the matter upon the Government and they cabled Sir George Perley, who represents Argenteuil, to urge upon the Government to award the contract.

Then I cannot understand how this contractor brought some tools and machinery to Grenville and expected to start on the work. I thought he had been notified that his tender had been accepted, but that the contract had not been signed.

As to the right of way,
before the election of 1911, a certain right of way through the mill property of the Hawkesbury Lumber Company had been expropriated. After the change of Government, the right of way was changed, and I understand that the other right of way, which the company now wish the Government to take, will be just as convenient for the public, but I would like to know

whether this new right of way has been deeded over to the Government or expropriated?

A new set of plans
has recently been made for a new right of way. ' I do not know whether it covers a portion of what my hon. friend has in mind or not.
I know that the engineers of the department either last summer or the summer before surveyed a new right of way. Has it been acquired by the Government or expropriated?
We will look up the information for my hon. friend. I am not clear on the point.
I would like to know also what compensation the company is asking for, the other right of way, In 1911, the Government offered $5,000.
Was that not considered enough?

The company was not objecting so much to the amount, but it had objected to the location of the right of way, and the matter has not yet been decided by the Exchequer Court. After September, 1911, I understand, the company prevailed upon the Government to change the right of way. I put a question on the Order Paper to ascertain what compensation was paid by the Government, and the answer was that no compensation was paid, that the right of way had been expropriated. I do not understand how it could have been expropriated without compensation.
Probably it has not been settled by the Exchequer Court up to date.
I suppose the department would say that the survey had been registered, and the Exchequer Court had not yet settled the amount. What amount does the department offer the company?
Somewhere about $5,000.
Do they refuse to accept that?
Evidently, or we should not have gone to the court.
I hope my hon. friend will get the information.

I desire to call the attention of the minister to the request repeatedly made by the people of Campbellton and Bonaventure opposite for a bridge across the Restigouche river. Seven or
eight years ago a Bill was passed to erect a joint highway and railway bridge at this point to connect the Gaspe system of railways and the Intercolonial. Fifty thousand dollars was voted as a subsidy. But this was deemed insufficient, and it was not found possible to float the securities necessary for the work. Meantime, the change of Administration took place. Since that time, the people on both sides, apparently assuming that the prospect of the joint highway and railway bridge was rather remote, organized a crusade in favour of a purely highway bridge. Deputations have come to Ottawa, and I understand that the Campbellton Board of Trade and all the municipal councils concerned have joined in this request. I understand that the last move made by the minister or the department, in answer to the deputation, was to instruct Mr. Stead, the department engineer for New Brunswick, to report upon this project of a highway bridge. Has any progress been made in ascertaining the cost? Has the department abandoned the policy of a joint railway and highway bridge and decided to limit itself to the highway bridge? The time will come when a railway bridge will be needed at this point to connect the Intercolonial with the Transcontinental and other railways.

We had a deputation here about a month ago of the different councils interested in this work. They pressed for a highway bridge. The information we have goes to show that this is a very, very expensive undertaking, much more expensive than was at first anticipated. After going into the facts with the deputation, it was decided that we should have a re-survey by Mr. Stead, who is supposed to be a first-class engineer, and Mr. Stead has undertaken that service. We shall not have his report for some considerable time. We thought it would be a good time to make u more extensive survey, in order to get at the facts in a detailed manner and t >
judge what is best in the public interest.
Has the department come to a conclusion as to building merely a highway bridge? Has the project to build a combined railway and highway bridgj been abandoned?
We have not come to any decision, and cannot arrive at a decision until we get the report of Mr. Stead showing the difference in the estimated cost of the two.

If a combined railway and highway bridge were built, it is calculated that Gaspe Basin, with a railway connection, would be brought into close communication with New England cities, especially with Boston, the great fish market for the United States. Gaspe and the whole Baie des Chaleurs district would be within twenty-four hours of Boston.
How many tenders were there for the substructure of the bridge at Hawkesbury?
Six.
What was the lowest?

I will give the hon. gentleman the list:	R. E. Sutherland, "Lind
say, $70,000; Galbraith, $78,000; Kennedy Construction Company, Montreal, $78,000; Jones Company, Limited, Ottawa, $90,000; Doney & McDonald, Alexandria, $90,000; Thomas & Wood, $90,000.
The tender of Mr. Galbraith is $78,000, and there is one for $70,000. Which one is that?
Sutherland.
Is he the one who will get this contract?
If he is capable of doing the work, certainly.
Have the tenderers been notified that their tender is accepted?

Mr. Chairman, I am in perfect harmony with the few remarks made by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), regarding the road in Matapedia. Miniota-bridge to Indian reserve, $8,000.

This amount is required for the construction of a steel bridge across the Assiniboine river at Miniota, at an estimated cost of $25,000. A request for its construction was made on behalf of the Miniota municipality by letter dated

March 17. I am informed that the settlers are very anxious that the bridge shall be ready so that the spring crop may be carried over it. I do not know why we should be building a bridge there; this is the first I have heard of it.

The only reason for the Government's share in its construction is probably its connection with the Indian reserve. The Dominion Go' eminent is asked to pay $8,000 of the cost, the balance to be paid by the Provincial Government and the two municipalities concerned.

I am given information

Telegraph and telephone lines generally, $7;ooo.
Mr. M.cKENZIE:	Under this item I
would ask for some information about the telephone system in Nova Scotia, particularly in the island of Cape Breton. In 1911 provision was made for the building of a line-indeed, I think it was pretty well under way-between Baddeck and the northeast of Margaree and also from Baddeck to Little Narrows and from Little Narrows to McKay Point. I think the line has been
[Mr Rogers.]
completed from Baddeck to northeast of Margaree and from Baddeck to the Little Narrows. What has been done towards completing the line from Little Narrows to McKay's Point? There is a section of country there which is rather isolated from the rest of the country by an arm of the sea, and it is exceedingly difficult in some seasons of the year to communicate with the towns without a telephone or telegraph line. The intention was to give the people along that section of the country the benefit of a telephone line. The poles were got out, I think in 1911 or before, and I understand that the wire has been put on the ground. Has anything been done towards the erection of a line from Little Narrows to McKay's Point which is right opposite the shire town of Baddeck on the other side of that arm of Bras d'Or lake?
We do not appear to have any information about that with us to-night. I have asked the deputy to write to my hon. friend to-morrow and give him the particulars of the conditions.

The county of Victoria which I represent has not the benefit of competing telegraph lines like other counties in Cape Breton and all the counties in Nova Scotia. Most of them have the services of the Government line, the Western Union and the Canadian Pacific railway, all competing lines, giving a good service. But in Victoria we have only the one lone, solitary Government line and we have an extension of something over 100 miles from the shire town across to the extreme north end of the county with no means of communication except the Government telegraph line. Of course, we have the mails, but we have no telephone and no other telegraph system.
It is at the northern end of the county that the cable connects with the Magdalen Islands. Considerable business goes over that line. The minister will understand that, as we are dependent for rapid communication upon this one line, it is exceedingly important to the people of the county that the service should be well conducted. But I regret to say that it is not managed with that business style and acumen that I think should be shown in connection with so important a service. I am sorry that in this connection I have to bring to the notice of the minister something that is political in its character. I brought it to the attention of the minister last year, but I do not think anything has

been done about it. I am not bringing this matter up for the purpose of asking the minister to dismiss any of his officials. For one thing I would not expect him to appoint in the place of a dismissed official any friend of mine. But what I ask the minister to do is to discipline his officials so that there will be a proper management of the Government business. Without mentioning names, I submit to the minister that a message sent from Baddeck over this line to any part of the county is not regarded as private. The facilities furnished in connection with the office at Baddeck are of such a character that the service is not private. Perhaps the man in charge of the office does not get enough pay to keep it private, or to conduct it as business of this character should be conducted. I have already brought to the notice of the minister that, during a local election that was conducted in the county a year ago last February, this whole system-the only system in the county-was absolutely commandeered by the managers of that campaign ; they took it entirely under their "wn control, and for the month or so that the campaign was in progress they used the line for their own purposes with-11 p.m. out paying one cent to the Government for the service. I am rather sorry to find that as far as I can learn nothing has been done or said about this matter since I last brought it to the notice of the minister. We had a trial in the town of Baddeck in connection with that election, and the man whom the minister ha3 in charge	of	that work	went
on the stand, and of his own volition told under oath how 4 he took the responsibility of taking over that line as a piece of electioneering machinery while the campaign was on, and he swore that he did not charge any one of his friends one cent, and that he made no return to the Government. That evidence was given on oath before the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia. That is the condition of affairs in connection with the only telegraph service we have in the county; and I appeal to the minister whether that is satisfactory and as it ought to be. As a *sound, progressive business people we have a right to expect better things. We have a Tight to expect that not only the office at Baddeck but every office on the line shall be well conducted, and that the minister shall give strict orders that .such a thing as commandeering such an important piece of public property for the use of any party-I care not which-shall
not be tolerated for one moment. I trust it will never occur again.

I remember that the hon. *member brought this matter up last year. I do not think he has had any reason to complain of irregularities during the last year. I can assure my hon. friend that I gave strict instructions that such a state of affairs would not be tolerated. The telegraph service should be kept absolutely private for every citizen of the country, and I shall endeavour to see that it is kept private.

I find in the Auditor General's Report that over 2,000,000 feet of British Columbia fir was supplied for slides and booms on the St. Maurice river between Shawenegan Falls and Three Rivers, the price paid being $43 per M. feet. Were any tenders asked for this timber and who supplied it?
The chief engineer does not seem to have that information.

My reason for asking the question is this. Before the late Government went out of power, whenever any quantity of timber of that character was supplied, prices were asked for from lumbermen or from men handling that line of business. The gentleman who supplied the 2,000,000 feet of lumber and who got $9,000 for it is an undertaker. I have known him for a number of years and l)ie only knowledge he has of the lumber business is in the handling of caskets and coffins. I was wondering how he came to supply this Government with British Columbia fir, when he is not in the business at all.
We will have to have this matter looked into. It looks a bad case.

It is rather a bad case. 1 do not see how it can be that this gentleman, who has been doing nothing but performing the very painful duty of carrying people to their last resting-place, should all of a sudden bob up in Three Rivers and have the supplying of this lumber there. If the old practice had been followed and prices asked from the lumbermen at Three Rivers, which is an important lumbering centre, better prices could have been obtained, and in fact the transaction would not have looked as shady as it looks now. If I could get some explanation, I would be satisfied.
I told my !hon. friend that we have not the information here.
Can I get it later on?
